articles.title: Derrota de Trump e vitória de Lula enfraquecem direita nas Américas e vira oportunidade para presidente brasileiro pacificar país | G1
articles.body:
A derrota política sofrida pelo presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump , nas eleições de meio de mandato e a reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) no Brasil enfraquecem a direita nas Américas e abrem uma oportunidade para o brasileiro buscar a pacificação do país.

A avaliação é de assessores e interlocutores de Lula . Para eles, os dois movimentos colocam um freio na ofensiva da ala mais ideológica do governo Trump, que buscava ampliar a influência da direita nas Américas.

Os democratas conquistaram o controle da Câmara dos Representantes e do Senado dos Estados Unidos nas eleições realizadas nesta terça (3), retirando dos republicanos o domínio das duas Casas do Congresso.

No Brasil, Lula foi reeleito no segundo turno, realizado em 25 de outubro, ao derrotar o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Na avaliação dos auxiliares do presidente brasileiro, os resultados nos dois países dificultam uma tentativa de tornar a direita hegemônica na região.

Eles lembram ainda que governos de direita eleitos recentemente na América do Sul já enfrentam dificuldades internas, o que, na visão desses interlocutores, pode limitar a capacidade de articulação regional desse campo político.

Na Argentina, o presidente Javier Milei representa a direita. No Chile, José Antonio Kast, também de direita, assumiu a Presidência neste ano. Antes da eleição brasileira, o avanço conservador havia levado a direita a governar metade dos países da América do Sul.

Agora, segundo os assessores de Lula, o novo cenário cria uma oportunidade para que o presidente, em seu quarto mandato, busque reduzir a polarização política no Brasil e ampliar o isolamento dos setores mais radicais da direita.

Na avaliação desses interlocutores, Lula terá no próximo mandato a oportunidade de avançar numa agenda de pacificação que não conseguiu implementar plenamente durante o terceiro mandato e, com isso, tentar reduzir a força política do bolsonarismo.

articles.body:
Tennessee state Sen. Brent Taylor (R) is projected to win the state’s redistricted 9th Congressional District seat, replacing Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tenn.), who is retiring, according to Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s partner.

Taylor defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson, independent Dennis Jeffrey Clark and independent Michelle Head in this House race.

In the days leading up to Election Day, Taylor’s campaign was hit by controversy after the Nashville Scene published a report that alleged Taylor sent unsolicited nude photos as late as 2021 to people who were not his wife. He told The Scene his “wife is well aware of” the photos and “we’ve worked through it a long time ago.”

In another interview with WREG , Taylor said the report “signals where we are in the campaign and who the frontrunner is with just seven days left in the campaign.”

“I’m willing to acknowledge my past indiscretions,” he said, frustrated “that my wife now has to relive something that we’ve already worked through together and moved on from.”

Taylor also benefitted from a gerrymandering effort — backed by President Trump — that favored the GOP in Tennessee. Cohen criticized the move , blasting Republicans for orchestrating what he called a power grab to disenfranchise Black voters in districts like his.

Cohen said his decision to retire from the House was driven by this maneuver, telling reporters earlier this year outside the House Rayburn building that he was “not a quitter” but “these districts were drawn to defeat me.”

While on the campaign trail, Taylor touted his record as a successful small-business owner; he and his wife own multiple funeral homes in Tennessee. He campaigned on combating high grocery and gas prices, lowering energy costs, reducing federal spending and securing the Southern border, according to his campaign website .

articles.title: Musk-aligned lawyer to succeed McCaul in House
articles.summary: Chris Gober (R) is projected to defeat Caitlin Rourk (D) in Texas’s 10th District, according to Decision Desk HQ. Gober will succeed Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas). McCaul, the 64-year-old former chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, is departing Congress after more than two decades on Capitol Hill. A graduate of Harvard Law School, Gober…
articles.body:
Chris Gober (R) is projected to defeat Caitlin Rourk (D) in Texas’s 10th District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Gober will succeed Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas). McCaul, the 64-year-old former chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, is departing Congress after more than two decades on Capitol Hill.

A graduate of Harvard Law School, Gober worked as a counsel in the Office of Legal Policy at the Department of Justice (DOJ) during former President George W. Bush’s tenure.

After leaving the DOJ, Gober worked at the Republican National Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee. He then entered the private legal sector, briefly returning to politics as general counsel for Sen. Ted Cruz’s (R-Texas) unsuccessful 2016 presidential campaign.

Gober then aligned himself with tech mogul Elon Musk, as the chief lawyer of the trillionaire’s America PAC. The committee spent hundreds of millions in support of President Trump’s 2024 campaign.

On the campaign trail, Gober vowed to lower the cost of living, secure the border and “protect” rural farms and ranches in his district. The safely red 10th District, which was left mostly unchanged after state lawmakers redistricted last year , includes suburbs of Houston and Austin.

Rourk is a member of the Army Reserve who worked in the communications division at Dell Technologies.

articles.title: La primera gran derrota de Trump en las 'midterms' de Estados Unidos: los demócratas ganan el Senado y logran el Congreso
articles.standfirst: Históricas victorias de la oposición en feudos conservadores como Texas o Iowa abren la puerta al primer presidente negro de la Cámara de Representantes
articles.summary: Históricas victorias de la oposición en feudos conservadores como Texas o Iowa abren la puerta al primer presidente negro de la Cámara de Representantes
articles.body: Las elecciones de mitad de mandato (midterms, en inglés) celebradas este martes en Estados Unidos han dejado un duro revés para Donald Trump. Los demócratas han logrado recuperar el control del Senado federal y van camino de amarrar también la Cámara de Representantes. Este vuelco electoral interrumpe el dominio total que los republicanos ejercían en Washington y abre una nueva fase en la que el presidente afrontará una fuerte oposición parlamentaria en los dos últimos años de su mandato. El descontento popular ha sido la clave del cambio de rumbo. A diferencia de las elecciones europeas, el votante estadounidense suele utilizar estas citas legislativas para examinar la gestión de la Casa Blanca. El fuerte encarecimiento de la vida, la percepción de corrupción gubernamental y la preocupación por el conflicto bélico en Irán han generado un malestar profundo que la intensa campaña de Trump no ha logrado mitigar, perdiendo incluso feudos tradicionalmente conservadores como Texas o Iowa. Para el ciudadano español, el resultado equivale a un escenario de "cohabitación" o bloqueo institucional. Sin la mayoría del Congreso a su favor, el mandatario republicano no podrá aprobar sus reformas con facilidad. Como contramedida, el magnate ya ha avisado de que recurrirá a su derecho de veto para paralizar los proyectos ley impulsados por la oposición, mientras que en el ámbito de su propia formación ha optado por distanciarse de los resultados argumentando que él no figuraba directamente en las papeletas. El cambio de mayorías transformará de inmediato el día a día en Washington mediante el uso de la supervisión parlamentaria. Las comisiones del Congreso, ahora encabezadas por la oposición, prevén abrir investigaciones sobre el patrimonio familiar del presidente y poner bajo la lupa a figuras de su entorno, entre las que destacan el secretario de Defensa, Pete Hegseth, o el magnate Elon Musk. El mapa político regional también ha registrado giros significativos durante la jornada, en la que se elegían 36 gobernadores. Los demócratas han conservado plazas clave como Pensilvania o Nueva York y han arrebatado el gobierno de Texas a los republicanos. La cita electoral deja además hitos como la elección de Keisha Lance Bottoms en Georgia, la primera mujer negra al frente de una gubernatura, o el triunfo de Byron Donalds en Florida. Con este nuevo tablero, el líder demócrata en la Cámara de Representantes, Hakeem Jeffries, perfila una agenda volcada en reducir el coste de vida y fiscalizar a la Casa Blanca. Por su parte, la contundente victoria de la oposición debilita la posición de cara a las presidenciales de figuras afines a la línea oficialista, como el vicepresidente JD Vance, redibujando el panorama para la recta final de la legislatura.

articles.title: Valadao ousted in battleground California House contest
articles.summary: Progressive challenger Randy Villegas (D) has defeated Rep. David Valadeo (R-Calif.) in the race for California’s 22nd Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ has projected. Villegas’s defeat of Valadeo knocks out an incumbent that has served in the House on and off from 2013 on, representing both the 22nd District and 21st District. The Democratic representative-elect…
articles.body:
Progressive challenger Randy Villegas (D) has defeated Rep. David Valadeo (R-Calif.) in the race for California’s 22nd Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ has projected.

Villegas’s defeat of Valadeo knocks out an incumbent that has served in the House on and off from 2013 on, representing both the 22nd District and 21st District. The Democratic representative-elect is an educator and activist who was victorious in his primary against California State Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains (D).

Villegas notched 65 percent support with 19 percent of the vote reported. Valadao garnered 35 percent support, per DDHQ.

During his primary , Villegas was endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).

Villegas is the child of immigrants from Mexico and teaches at a community college named College of the Sequoias. He is a graduate of the University of California Santa Cruz, earning a PhD from the school in 2020, and is the first member of his family to graduate from college, according to Mother Jones.

The race between Valadeo and Villegas had been rated as a “toss up” by the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report, while Decision Desk HQ had rated the race as “likely” Democratic.

Villegas’s opponent, Valadeo, distanced himself from President Trump after being one of the 10 Republicans that voted to impeach the president following the Jan. 6, 2021 attacks on the U.S. Capitol.

articles.title: Ricketts wins reelection over independent Osborn in Nebraska Senate race
articles.summary: Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) fended off a Senate challenge from independent Dan Osborn, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects, keeping the Nebraska seat under GOP control. Ricketts, who won the 2024 race to fill out the remainder of former Sen. Ben Sasse’s (R-Neb.) term, was the favorite to win a full six years in the upper…
articles.body:
Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) fended off a Senate challenge from independent Dan Osborn, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects, keeping the Nebraska seat under GOP control.

Ricketts, who won the 2024 race to fill out the remainder of former Sen. Ben Sasse’s (R-Neb.) term, was the favorite to win a full six years in the upper chamber.

Ricketts garnered about 49 percent of the vote, while Osborn notched just over 45 percent with 41 percent of the vote reported as of early Wednesday.

But Osborn, an Independent who came within 7 percentage points of Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) in 2024’s race , put up another tough fight in the Cornhusker State, where Republicans have dominated the congressional delegation and governorship for decades.

GOP voters make up roughly half of registered voters in Nebraska, and Democrats make up just a quarter . Osborn promised not to caucus with either party if elected.

But Ricketts and other Republicans argued that Osborn was a Democrat in disguise, pointing to his support from the state party.

Nebraska Democrats, who put up a write-in candidate after a spat with Osborn in 2024, rallied behind him this cycle. Their 2026 nominee, Cindy Burbank, dropped out after the primary to clear a path for the independent .

President Trump, who supported Ricketts, visited Nebraska as part of his red-state blitz in the weeks ahead of the election — a move operatives in the state saw as a sign that Republicans were worried about the race.

Despite Republicans’ advantage in Nebraska congressional races, the state has a more dynamic record in the presidential race.

Its “blue dot” district in the Omaha area, the 2nd Congressional District, has been a swing seat in recent elections and went to former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 White House race, even as Nebraska’s other two districts went red. One of only two states that split their Electoral College votes based on individual district results, the seat added to Harris’s tally.

articles.title: Navy admiral fired by Hegseth flips Mace’s South Carolina seat
articles.summary: Democrat Nancy Lacore, a former Navy Admiral who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is projected to win in the traditionally red House district in South Carolina against Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted the race for Rep. Nancy Mace’s (R) 1st District…
articles.body:
Democrat Nancy Lacore, a former Navy Admiral who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is projected to win in the traditionally red House district in South Carolina against Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted the race for Rep. Nancy Mace’s (R) 1st District seat from “lean Republican” to a “toss-up,” as Lacore out-fundraised Honeycutt, a Charleston County Council member. Mace unsuccessfully ran for governor in the Palmetto State earlier this year.

The Democrat notched just under 50 percent of the vote, while Honeycutt trailed by over 48 percent, with all votes tallied as of early Wednesday.

On the campaign trail, Lacore criticized Hegseth’s management of the Pentagon and painted him as the public face of the increasingly unpopular Iran war, which resonated with voters in a district President Trump won by 13 percentage points two years ago.

Lacore, who spent more than three decades in the Navy, started as a helicopter pilot and rose through the ranks to eventually become the chief of Navy Reserve, where she oversaw more than 60,000 sailors.

She completed two deployments and has used her defense-focused background to connect with voters wary of Hegseth’s handling of the Defense Department.

This summer, Lacore was locked in a tough primary race with Democrat Mac Deford, eventually beating the Coast Guard veteran in a June runoff and advancing to the general election in a district that was recently gerrymandered to favor the GOP.

articles.title: Democrat flips Gonzales’s former House seat in Texas
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Senate candidate Katy Padilla Stout is projected to win the Lone Star State’s open seat for the 23rd Congressional District vacated by former Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas), according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ. Padilla Stout defeated YouTube personality Brandon Herrera (R), an outspoken firearms advocate with President Trump’s endorsement. She ran…
articles.body:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate Katy Padilla Stout is projected to win the Lone Star State’s open seat for the 23rd Congressional District vacated by former Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas), according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ.

Padilla Stout defeated YouTube personality Brandon Herrera (R), an outspoken firearms advocate with President Trump’s endorsement. She ran in a district that the election handicapper Cook Political Report predicted would be a likely win for Herrera.

She notched almost 52 percent while Herrera garnered about 44 percent, with 55 percent of the vote reported early Wednesday.

Gonzales departed the House in April following a reported affair with a staffer who later died by suicide. Facing growing calls for resignation or expulsion based on allegations of sexual misconduct, Gonzales said he would “file my retirement from office.”

Padilla Stout campaigned on improving the affordability of healthcare and called on Congress to take bipartisan action to keep the southern border secure, but also to allow for more “reasonable and humane immigration laws,” including fair methods to make the pathway to citizenship simple but reasonable, according to her campaign website.

The Texas Democrat previously worked as an attorney at a family legal practice representing foster children.

National Democratic Party operatives channeled more effort into the race following her win against three other Democrats during the primary, the San Antonio Express-News reported . The party funneled millions of dollars to back her campaign, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg stumping for Padilla Stout on the campaign trail.

Padilla Stout told The American Prospect that Democrats would need to earn voters’ trust, leading her to organize with other candidates across the state to canvass for support.

“We’ve allowed leaders on both sides of the aisle to not have to answer to their constituents,” she told the outlet. “The people are the boss … not the other way around.”

articles.title: Knickerbocker defeats Turner, flips Ohio House seat for Democrats
articles.summary: Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker is projected to win Ohio’s 10th District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Knickerbocker defeated longtime Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio) in a district the incumbent comfortably held for more than two decades. The Democrat garnered just over 49 percent of the vote while the incumbent notched nearly 48 percent, with 65 percent…
articles.body:
Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker is projected to win Ohio’s 10th District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Knickerbocker defeated longtime Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio) in a district the incumbent comfortably held for more than two decades. The Democrat garnered just over 49 percent of the vote while the incumbent notched nearly 48 percent, with 65 percent of the vote reported early Wednesday.

Turner, a former mayor of Dayton, Ohio, was first elected to Congress in 2002 and most recently won reelection in 2024 by roughly 18 percentage points. But this year’s contest proved to be a different story.

Knickerbocker, a veteran, entered the race as a first-time congressional candidate, hoping to capitalize on growing frustration over affordability and President Trump’s economic policies.

DDHQ rated the seat “likely Republican” heading into Election Day.

The Democrat leaned heavily on her background in healthcare, emphasizing rising medical costs and access to treatment while criticizing federal spending cuts that she argued would hurt working families.

She secured the Democratic nomination in May after emerging from a crowded six-candidate primary.

Knickerbocker has worked as a neuro-oncology nurse practitioner at the Ohio State University’s Wexner Medical Center and served in both the Air Force and Air Force Reserve.

Turner, meanwhile, pointed to his experience in Washington, D.C., particularly on national security and defense issues. The Republican, who is backed by President Trump, previously chaired the House Intelligence Committee and has been a prominent voice on military policy.

articles.title: Louisiana 5th District House race proceeds to runoff
articles.summary: Democratic Louisiana state Rep. Patricia Moore and Republican state Rep. Gabe Firment are projected to advance to a runoff in Louisiana’s 5th House District race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Moore had less than a one percentage point advantage over Firment as of 12:53 a.m. with 93 percent of votes in on Wednesday morning,…
articles.body:
Democratic Louisiana state Rep. Patricia Moore and Republican state Rep. Gabe Firment are projected to advance to a runoff in Louisiana’s 5th House District race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Moore had less than a one percentage point advantage over Firment as of 12:53 a.m. with 93 percent of votes in on Wednesday morning, according to DDHQ. Both candidates received just under 18 percent of the vote each, with the remaining vote total split among seven other candidates.

The two candidates will proceed to a runoff on Dec. 12 to determine who will replace GOP Rep. Julia Letlow, after she left her seat to launch a successful bid for Senate.

The 5th District encompasses portions of northeastern and central Louisiana. The primary race in this district was canceled after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the state’s new GOP-drawn map was an unconstitutional gerrymander.

Moore was elected to the Louisiana House in 2019 and has advocated for protecting and expanding healthcare access, investing in small businesses and lowering everyday costs, according to her campaign website .

Firment has served in the Louisiana House for six years, where he chairs the state House Insurance Committee. He campaigned on lowering taxes, strengthening public safety, safeguarding Social Security and Medicare benefits and protecting Second Amendment rights.

articles.title: What to know about James Talarico's girlfriend and family
articles.summary: James Talarico delivered a long-coveted win in Texas for Democrats. Here's what to know about his girlfriend and family.
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' U.S. Senate race on Nov. 3, a major political upset, the Associated Press and NBC News projected.

His victory gave Democrats the statewide win in Texas they had chased for years, particularly since Beto O'Rourke nearly unseated Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018. Talarico will head to Washington, DC, with his longtime girlfriend, Brianna Menard.

Talarico called Menard "his rock" during an appearance on The Jamie Kern Lima Show podcast. "I don't know if I could have gotten through the last six months of this crazy race if she hadn't been by my side," he said.

Here's what you need to know about Menard.

Talarico's partner worked for him as chief of staff

Menard met Talarico while working as his chief of staff, Talarico said on "The Jamie Kern Lima Show." His campaign confirmed their relationship to The New York Times in August.

"Four years ago, after he and his then-chief of staff developed feelings for each other and started dating, she left the office to pursue other opportunities," a Talarico campaign spokesman told the Times.

After departing Talarico's office, Menard worked to elect state Rep. Salman Bhojani, the first Muslim member of the Texas legislature, before becoming his chief of staff, according to a 2023 post on X by Talarico .

She currently works as the director of TEXPAC and Political Education at the Texas Medical Association, according to her biography page on the committee's website. The group describes itself as a "bipartisan political action committee" with the goal of electing "medicine-friendly candidates at the state and federal levels."

Byron Donalds celebrates historic victory as Florida’s first Black governor

Menard's veganism target of Paxton attacks

Throughout the campaign, Paxton attacked Talarico's masculinity and claimed that the now senator-elect was a vegan.

Talarico denied that he had ever been a vegan, with a campaign spokesperson telling the New York Post: "James is not and never has been a vegan, much to his girlfriend's chagrin. As the saying goes, true love conquers all."

The Post reported that Menard described herself as a "committed vegan" in a since-deleted biography page of an Austin grocery co-op. Talarico said on "The Jamie Kern Lima Show" that Menard did not "want any part of" the contentious campaign but is "very supportive."

"What I'm trying to do is protect her and my family and my friends from the impacts of this race, because I signed up to run for the U.S. Senate. Obviously, they did not, and so I'm trying to balance running this race while also protecting them and protecting her in particular," he said.

What to know about James Talarico's family

Talarico was born in 1989 in Round Rock, Texas, to a single mother, according to his campaign website . After his father became abusive, his mother moved them to a hotel, and later an apartment, and raised Talarico in East Austin.

His adoptive father, Mark Talarico, met James Talarico's mother shortly after she fled his birth father, according to a Texas Monthly profile. The couple married within a year.

"I would not be a state legislator or a pastor or anything like that if I had not met Mark Talarico," Talarico said.

He was contacted by a member of his birth father's family as a young adult but declined, he told Texas Monthly.

Contributing: Nicole Fallert , USA TODAY

articles.title: Missouri voters reject new GOP-friendly House map
articles.summary: A ballot measure that looks to enact a more Republican-friendly House map in Missouri is projected to fail, delivering a major win for Democrats, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Voters rejected the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, which would have allowed lawmakers to pass a new set of congressional lines ahead of the…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that looks to enact a more Republican-friendly House map in Missouri is projected to fail, delivering a major win for Democrats, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Voters rejected the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, which would have allowed lawmakers to pass a new set of congressional lines ahead of the next U.S. census that would have weakened Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) Kansas City-based district and given Republicans a new House pickup opportunity .

The proposition is projected to fail by double digits, with over 60 percent opposing the measure with just 15 percent of the vote reported early Wednesday morning.

The GOP has a 6-2 edge in Missouri’s congressional delegation, but the new map would usher in a 7-1 Republican-favored House delegation after 2028. Rep. Wesley Bell’s (D-Mo.) St. Louis-area House seat would be the lone Democratic district.

The failed passage of the new district lines means that Missouri will operate under the same districts it had in recent past cycles.

Missouri has served as ground zero for a national redistricting saga that’s played out between Republican and Democratic states. President Trump and national Republicans encouraged GOP lawmakers in states like Texas and Missouri to redraw their maps to create new pickup opportunities for their party as Republicans braced for a competitive midterm environment.

Democrats in other states responded in kind, though they were only successful at creating new maps in California ahead of the 2026 elections.

The battle in Missouri was particularly fierce amid litigation over whether the new House maps could be enacted in time for November as a coalition looked to put the new congressional lines to a referendum, stalling the House map’s immediate implementation.

The state’s high court, made up of a majority of appointees by Republican governors, ruled in September that the GOP-favorable map could not immediately go into effect until voters weighed in on the new lines in November. The litigation made it all the way up to the Supreme Court several times but to no avail for the GOP.

articles.title: Missouri rejects ballot measure to overturn abortion protections
articles.summary: Missouri voted to protect abortion access Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ projects, narrowly rejecting a ballot measure that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban just two years after it was overturned. Missouri in 2024 became the first state to use a ballot measure to overturn a near-total abortion ban and put a reproductive freedom amendment…
articles.body:
Missouri voted to protect abortion access Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ projects, narrowly rejecting a ballot measure that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban just two years after it was overturned.

Missouri in 2024 became the first state to use a ballot measure to overturn a near-total abortion ban and put a reproductive freedom amendment in the state constitution. That measure, also called Amendment 3, was approved by a narrow 51.6 percent majority.

Nearly 54 percent of voters rejected the measure, with 15 percent of the vote reported.

The GOP-dominated legislature, furious at the result, set out to change it. They used a legislative maneuver to place a question on the ballot that would rescind abortion rights, as well as restrict gender-affirming drugs and surgery for minors.

Opponents said Republicans tried to mislead voters by packaging an anti-transgender measure with the abortion ban — an effort critics called “ballot candy”— and recycling the same amendment name from the last election. In 2024, a “yes” vote on Amendment 3 repealed the state’s abortion ban. This year, a “yes” vote reinstated it.

The state’s 2022 law was the strictest in the country, with no exceptions for rape or incest. Supporters of the ballot measure argued that the new language is less restrictive and better reflects what voters intended in 2024.

Unlike the law that was passed in the wake of the Dobbs decision in 2022, Amendment 3 includes limited exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies (birth defect or congenital disorder), and for survivors of rape or incest only up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

The measure would also have enacted a constitutional ban on gender transition surgery for minors as well as the prescription or administration of cross-sex hormones or puberty-blocking drugs to minors — though both are already banned by law.

articles.title: West Virginia approves citizenship voting ballot measure

articles.body:
A ballot measure that would specify that only U.S. citizens are allowed to vote in elections in West Virginia is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The constitutional amendment, known as Amendment 1, makes a change to the language of the West Virginia Constitution. It currently reads, “the citizens of the State shall be entitled to vote at all elections held within the counties in which they respectively reside,” but it will shift to “only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state shall be entitled to vote at all elections held within the counties in which they respectively reside.”

The ballot measure is projected to pass with nearly 80 percent support, with almost all of the vote reported as of early Wednesday.

West Virginia law already requires voters to be U.S. citizens to vote in the state, but this ballot measure would add the requirement to the state constitution.

Noncitizens are not allowed to vote in federal elections, and only a small group of municipalities in addition to Washington, D.C., allow noncitizens to vote in certain elections, according to Ballotpedia .

Republicans have leaned into issues around voting and proper identification, particularly as President Trump has asserted without basis that there has been widespread voter fraud in the U.S.

The president has pressed GOP lawmakers to pass legislation that would require people to show proof of citizenship in order to register to vote and show photo identification at the polls, though those efforts have been unsuccessful.

Ballotpedia notes that more than a dozen states are teeing up ballot measures Tuesday pertaining to election policy, including six states that are asking voters about voting and citizenship and six states asking about voter ID.

articles.title: South Dakota approves ballot measure affirming only citizens can vote in elections
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would affirm that only U.S. citizens can vote in elections in South Dakota is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ. articles.body:
A ballot measure that would affirm that only U.S. citizens can vote in elections in South Dakota is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The constitutional amendment, assigned the letter “J” on the ballot, changes the South Dakota Constitution to make it clear that only U.S. citizens are allowed to vote in races in the state, adding the line, “An individual who is not a citizen of the United States is disqualified from voting in any election or upon any question submitted to the voters of this state.”

Nearly 62 percent of voters backed the measure, with 84 percent reported.

It also clarifies that “an individual may be disqualified by law for mental incompetence or the conviction of a felony.”

South Dakota’s Constitution already makes it clear that voters must be U.S. citizens to be eligible to vote, saying, “Every United States citizen eighteen years of age or older who has met all residency and registration requirements shall be entitled to vote in all elections and upon all questions submitted to the voters of the state unless disqualified by law for mental incompetence or the conviction of a felony.”

The ballot measure looks to reiterate the citizenship voting requirement even further.

Republicans have leaned into issues around voting and proper identification, particularly as President Trump has baselessly asserted there’s been widespread voter fraud in the U.S.

The president has pressed GOP lawmakers to pass legislation that would require people to show proof of citizenship in order to register to vote and show photo identification at the polls, though those efforts have been unsuccessful.

Ballotpedia notes that more than a dozen states teed up ballot measures Tuesday pertaining to election policy, including six states that are asking voters about citizenship and six states asking about voter ID.

articles.title: Massachusetts voters reject ballot measure eliminating jungle primaries
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would have eliminated party primary elections from being held in Massachusetts is projected to fail, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ. Question 3 would have allowed candidates from all parties to appear on the primary ballot, with the top two candidates advancing to the general election based on primary…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would have eliminated party primary elections from being held in Massachusetts is projected to fail, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ.

Question 3 would have allowed candidates from all parties to appear on the primary ballot, with the top two candidates advancing to the general election based on primary results. Approving Question 3 would have opened up the possibility that two candidates from the same party could run against each other in the general election.

About 61 percent of voters opposed the measure, with 69 percent of the vote reported as of early Wednesday.

Question 3’s supporters include the NAACP of New England and a bipartisan coalition of mayors, progressive groups and Republicans, Boston-based NPR affiliate WBUR reported . But it similarly received opposition from bipartisan groups, including several unions and state Republican Party and Democratic Party officials.

The measure received financial funding from the Coalition for Healthy Democracy 2026 , which channeled $4 million into the campaign, the most of any ballot question on the Bay State’s ballot during this election cycle, Boston radio station WGBH reported .

Other supporters included former Massachusetts Govs. Charlie Baker (R) and Deval Patrick (D) and Joshua Bekenstein, a co-founder of the venture capital firm Bain Capital, who contributed $500,000.

Those who funded the opposing campaign included Voter Rights MA, the Massachusetts Democratic Party State Committee and the union SEIU 1099, which spent $100,000 against Question 3.

Massachusetts adopted partisan primaries in 1911, changing the practice of the time in which political parties controlled how candidates were nominated to represent the party in elections, according to Massachusetts Secretary of State Bill Galvin’s (D) office.

Massachusetts joins California and Washington as the only three states to allow jungle primaries for statewide offices and congressional races.

articles.title: DC approves ballot measure banning foie gras from local restaurants
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would ban foie gras — a luxury delicacy associated with French cuisine made from the liver of a duck or goose fattened by force feeding — from being served in local restaurants is projected to pass in Washington, D.C., according to Decision Desk HQ. Initiative 86, called the “Prohibiting Force-Feeding of…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would ban foie gras — a luxury delicacy associated with French cuisine made from the liver of a duck or goose fattened by force feeding — from being served in local restaurants is projected to pass in Washington, D.C., according to Decision Desk HQ.

Initiative 86, called the “Prohibiting Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026,” prohibits the sale and distribution of fattened-bird-liver products, as well as the practice of force-feeding birds to enlarge their lives, within the District.

About 73 percent of voters backed the measure, according to Decision Desk HQ early Wednesday.

The D.C. Board of Elections placed the initiative on the ballot in August after proponents of the ban collected enough signatures .

The initiative has become one of the most contentious issues on D.C. voters’ November ballots. In the traditionally blue District, the Democratic nominees for its elected offices are expected to win comfortably, including Janeese Lewis George, the democratic socialist who’s the Democratic nominee to succeed three-term Mayor Muriel Bowser.

The proposed ban pitted animal rights advocates against the city’s fine dining industry.

The initiative was backed by Pro-Animal DC, an animal advocacy group that submitted more than 45,000 signatures to ban the “sale or distribution of any product resulting from force-feeding a bird, including foie gras.”

Supporters argue the force-feeding process causes unnecessary suffering by repeatedly feeding ducks or geese large amounts of food until their liver becomes enlarged.

The initiative drew opposition from restaurants and butchers that sell foie gras. In an op-ed in The Washington Post , Butterworth’s chef and owner, Bart Hutchins, said that he was “incredibly disappointed” that the measure made the ballot.

Restaurants and retailers that violate the law could face fines ranging from $1,000 to $5,000, while repeat offenders could result in the suspension of their business license.

A foie gras ban in California was enacted in 2012. California’s bill was declined for review by the Supreme Court twice, but the product has still been spotted in stores throughout the state, according to a 2025 article from Los Angeles Times.

The ban in D.C. will go into July 1, 2027.

articles.title: Forstag flips Montana House seat, beating Trump-backed opponent
articles.summary: Democrat Sam Forstag is the projected winner of the election for Montana’s 1st District, a key flip in his party’s push to take control of the House, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Forstag, a former smokejumper and union leader, defeated Republican challenger Aaron Flint, a retired Army lieutenant colonel, in the race for the open seat — a…
articles.body:
Democrat Sam Forstag is the projected winner of the election for Montana’s 1st District, a key flip in his party’s push to take control of the House, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Forstag, a former smokejumper and union leader, defeated Republican challenger Aaron Flint, a retired Army lieutenant colonel, in the race for the open seat — a district that the city of Missoula and covers the western portion of the state. The Democrat will replace retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke.

The Democrat led Flint by over 10 percentage points with just 10 percent of the vote reported — 54 to 43 percent, according to Decision Desk HQ early Wednesday.

The win is a blow to Republicans, whom DDHQ favored to hold onto the seat ahead of Election Day. While most election handicappers forecasted the seat would likely remain in GOP hands, Cook Political Report changed the race to a “toss up” in mid-October, saying at the time the Democrat had “a clear shot” at snatching the seat — a forecast which proved correct.

President Trump won the district by 11 points in the last election.

The Democrat emphasized his working-class background and union leadership throughout the campaign trail, racking up endorsements from several labor groups. He also earned the backing of former Montana Gov. Marc Racicot (R).

Critics, however, slammed Forstag’s background as a lobbyist, with the conservative Leadership in Action PAC releasing an attack ad tying $249,000 in lobbying fees to his work in Washington.

articles.title: 5 takeaways on a midterm rout for Democrats
articles.summary: Tuesday saw seismic results in the midterm elections as Democrats virtually ran the table of competitive races, and voters delivered a powerful rebuke to President Trump and the GOP. The bottom line is that Democrats have won control of the Senate and the House. And while the precise tally in each chamber remains unclear, the…
articles.body:
Tuesday saw seismic results in the midterm elections as Democrats virtually ran the table of competitive races, and voters delivered a powerful rebuke to President Trump and the GOP.

The bottom line is that Democrats have won control of the Senate and the House. And while the precise tally in each chamber remains unclear, the party will have bigger majorities than many were projecting just weeks ago.

Trump sought to pin the blame on Republican candidates — a case he made on social media and in a midnight interview with Fox News.

But plenty of people in his party are murmuring about his role in the debacle, given his low approval ratings and the fact that his preferred candidates in key Senate races went down in defeat.

There are other questions only time will answer, including what Democrats will do with their newfound power, and what impact the results will have on the 2028 race for the White House.

But here are the main takeaways from Tuesday.

Democrats had gone into Tuesday buoyed by strong opinion polls and by the belief that the nation was growing tired of Trump’s antics amid worries about the economy.

But liberal America had also grown nervous about elections, wounded by Trump’s 2016 and 2024 victories, and cognizant of his propensity to outperform the polls.

In the end, the night could hardly have gone better for Democrats.

In the battle for the Senate, they won, or are set to win, virtually every competitive race.

Seats that seemed at the outer edges of their ambitions, including in South Carolina and Kansas, have turned blue. Adam Hamilton’s victory over Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) was the first Democratic Senate victory in Kansas in almost 100 years.

Democrats have 54 seats in the Senate, with races in Alaska and Mississippi still too early or too close to call.

In the House, where Democrats were reasonably confident of achieving the 218 seats needed to take the majority, they went way beyond their mark. As of 1 a.m. ET, The Hill’s data and polling partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) was projecting that Democrats would win 256 seats, a majority just shy of the high watermark during the Obama years.

Before Tuesday, some experts had suggested that wave elections were a thing of the past, thanks to a combination of deepening polarization and partisan gerrymandering. The voters proved that wrong. This was a Democratic tsunami.

The president told his supporters to vote as if he was on the ballot. He toured the country for rallies targeted to rev up the MAGA base. He assailed Democrats in language that was inflammatory even by his standards.

Voter dissatisfaction over the cost of living, the economy, the war in Iran and Trump himself all proved too strong to overcome.

At one level, perhaps that should not have been a surprise. The DDHQ polling average puts Trump’s approval rating 20 points into negative territory. But Trump has defied the laws of political gravity before, and it was striking to see his party so comprehensively rebuked on Tuesday.

Trump tried to put distance between himself and the result.

“They didn’t like the candidates,” he mused during his Fox News interview.

On social media, he protested, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

Outside of the most fervent MAGA base, there are not many people who take such claims seriously.

The Lone Star State has dashed Democratic dreams several times in recent decades. The party’s hopes that figures like former Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) could win statewide races ran aground.

That all changed on Tuesday, when 37-year-old state Rep. James Talarico (D) emphatically defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the battle for a Senate seat. Even more shockingly to some, three-term Gov. Greg Abbott (R) was vanquished by state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D).

There will be deep Republican recriminations about the Senate race, where Trump was instrumental in Paxton’s defeat of incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R) in the GOP primary.

Plenty of Republicans had concerns from the get-go about Paxton’s checkered personal history, which includes settling charges of securities fraud, facing accusations of adultery and suffering impeachment by the state House.

Talarico prevailed with startling ease in the end. With 90 percent of ballots counted at 2 a.m. ET, he was ahead by roughly 10 points.

Abbott’s supporters figured he could draw on the strength of his political brand to escape any drag from Paxton and the national environment.

They were wrong. He has conceded the race to Hinojosa and looks on track to lose by about 7 points.

Democrats prevail in the most controversial races

Abdul El-Sayed was projected the winner of the Senate race in Michigan by DDHQ shortly before 1:30 a.m. ET.

The former public health official will become the nation’s first Muslim senator. He withstood extraordinary turbulence to get there — including the Democrat he defeated in the primary, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), endorsing his GOP opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), on Sunday.

El-Sayed also faced Islamophobic attacks from Trump, who repeatedly branded him a “jihadist.”

He was one of three Democrats who prevailed in especially contentious races.

Amy Acton (D) will be the next governor of Ohio after she beat GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy.

Their contest made national headlines after the Ramaswamy campaign ran an ad that featured Acton’s estranged mother calling her a “liar.” The backstory was even more disturbing. During Acton’s childhood, her stepfather had been charged with sexually abusing her. He skipped the state, accompanied by Acton’s mother, to avoid a full trial. The ad appeared to backfire, earning the condemnation of the current Republican governor, Mike DeWine, and his predecessor, John Kasich.

Meanwhile, in Texas, Trump’s nickname for Talarico (“Talafreako”) and insinuations about his sexuality from Republicans including Vice President Vance did little to damage his performance.

The polling industry will be breathing a sigh of relief. Another big miss would have seen fundamental questions grow sharper about their whole enterprise.

Counting was not complete in some of the most high-profile races in the early hours of Wednesday, making it hard to provide a precise accounting of how well the pollsters did.

But what matters is that their projections of a very good night for Democrats, which drew derision especially from some conservatives, were basically accurate.

Leticia Gutierrez (D) is projected to defeat Alex Mealer (R) in Texas’s 9th District, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Gutierrez is leading Mealer by 14 points with 78 percent reporting, per DDHQ.

Gutierrez will succeed Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) in representing the 9th District. After state lawmakers redrew Green’s Houston-area district last year to favor the GOP, Green lost to Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas) in the 18th District’s Democratic primary runoff .

Gutierrez is the former chief of staff for the Houston City Council and an environmental advocate. She secured 53 percent of the vote in a crowded Democratic primary to secure the nomination earlier this year.

Mealer served in the Army for five years, reaching the rank of captain. After her service ended, she worked in the investment banking sector in Houston, focusing on oil and gas transactions.

She also has local governing experience from her time as public safety chair on the board of the Metropolitan Transit Authority of Harris County in 2024 and 2025.

Mealer defeated Texas state Rep. Briscoe Cain (R) in the GOP primary runoff earlier this year with President Trump’s endorsement.

articles.body:
Jessica Steinmann (R) is projected to defeat Laura Jones (D) in Texas’s 8th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Steinmann leads Jones by about 10 points with 91 percent of the vote in, per DDHQ.

The constitutional lawyer will succeed Rep. Morgan Luttrell (R-Texas), a 50-year-old former Navy SEAL who is departing the lower chamber after one term.

Steinmann’s win, which came after she cruised to victory in the March Republican primary , is no surprise. She defeated Jones, a real estate agent, after Texas lawmakers last year slightly redrew the 8th District in the southeastern part of the state.

Steinmann was the director of the Justice Department’s Office of Victims of Crime during President Trump’s first term. Between the president’s initial and ongoing term, she was the executive general counsel at the America First Policy Institute.

In the latter role, Steinmann led legal challenges to Democratic policies across the country and sued Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg (D) over his eventually successful efforts to prosecute Trump .

Steinmann also helped draft a law that made significant changes to Texas’s voting system. The Lone Star State adopted the law in 2021, despite Democrats in the Texas Legislature fleeing the state in an attempt to block it.

On the campaign trail, Steinmann aligned herself with the MAGA movement, touting endorsements from Trump, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas).

She also pushed back on diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, vowed to bar transgender girls from playing women’s sports and backed Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration.

A ballot measure that would introduce minor language changes to an Alaska law around citizenship and voter eligibility is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The effort, dubbed Initiative Petition 25USCV, notes that Alaska law mandates that voters must be citizens and meet other criteria in order to be eligible to vote. It is projected to pass with nearly 70 percent support, with 69 percent of the report tallied by DDHQ.

The measure asked voters if they would approve an initiative to “specify that only those who are United States citizens and meet the other requirements may vote,” essentially adding the word “only” to current Alaska law .

The current language says “a person may vote at any election” if they meet the state’s criteria.

The ballot measure itself will not change voting requirements in the Last Frontier and only introduces the minor addition to the statue language. It required a simple majority to pass.

Noncitizens are not allowed to vote in federal elections, and only a small group of municipalities in addition to Washington, D.C., allow them to vote in certain elections, according to Ballotpedia .

Republicans have leaned into issues around voting and proper identification , particularly as President Trump has asserted without basis that there has been widespread voter fraud .

The president has pressed GOP lawmakers to pass legislation that would require people to show proof of citizenship in order to register to vote and show photo identification at the polls, though those efforts have been unsuccessful.

articles.body:
Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) is projected to win a 23rd term representing Ohio in the House, emerging from a tough rematch with Republican Derek Merrin, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Notching another two-year term in Ohio’s 9th Congressional District, Kaptur extends her record as the longest-serving woman in congressional history. She is projected to notch nearly 53 percent of the vote, with 10 percent of the vote reported as of early Wednesday.

The Democrat scraped by against Merrin by less than a percentage point in 2024, winning by just 2,382 votes .

A year later, Ohio underwent redistricting that squeezed Kaptur’s northwestern Ohio district: It voted for President Trump by 7 points in 2024 but would have backed him by 11 points under the new maps.

A Libertarian on the 2024 ballot was seen by some as a spoiler , but the third party’s candidate withdrew his 2026 bid, leaving Kaptur and Merrin alone on the ballot.

Merrin, who was a part of the Republican House campaign arm’s “MAGA Majority” program, was also boosted by Ohio visits from Trump and Vice President Vance as they sought to turn out Republicans for other tough Buckeye State races, including a battleground Senate contest between Democrat Sherrod Brown and Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

But although Tuesday’s race marked the most challenging of Kaptur’s career, she significantly outraised and outspent Merrin, a former state representative backed by Trump .

Heading into the race, DDHQ gave Kaptur an estimated 7 in 10 chance of winning.

articles.body:
A Nevada ballot measure that aims to add voter identification requirements when casting a ballot is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The constitutional amendment, known as Question 7, would add language to the state Constitution requiring someone to show photo identification if they voted in-person early or on Election Day.

The measure is projected to pass with 61 percent support, with 70 percent of the vote tally reported early Wednesday.

The ballot measure would require those who cast mail-in ballots to either include the last four digits of their Nevada driver’s license number, last four digits of their Social Security number (if they don’t have a driver’s license from the state) or “the number provided by the county clerk when the voter registered to vote” if someone has neither a Nevada driver’s license or Social Security number.

The ballot measure passed in 2024 with over 70 percent, but the initiative needs to be passed one more time in back-to-back consecutive election cycles in order for it to be implemented.

articles.body:
Nevada voters have approved a ballot measure protecting abortion up to the point of viability, officially adding the protection to the state constitution, Decision Desk HQ has projected.

The measure allows the state to enact restrictions after viability is reached, which is usually around the 24-week mark, except when necessary to protect the life or health of the mother. It is projected to pass with 63 percent support, with 70 percent of the vote reported early Wednesday.

This is the second straight election that Nevadans passed the measure , as constitutional amendments need to be approved in two even-numbered election years in a row. Nevadans voted in favor of the measure two years ago with 64 percent in favor.

The amendment’s passage continues the sweeping success for reproductive rights on the ballot in various states throughout the country since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. Different states, leaning both Democratic and Republican, have passed measures protecting abortion rights since then.

That includes states such as California, Vermont, Ohio and Missouri. More than a dozen states, mostly in the South, have implemented near-total abortion bans.

articles.title: Nebraska voters approve ban on transgender athletes in girls sports
articles.summary: A ballot measure requiring schools to designate “biological sexes” to sports teams, is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ. Voters approved the constitutional amendment, known as Initiative Measure 442, which would require public schools, both K-12 and colleges and universities — in addition to any private schools that compete against them — to…
articles.body:
A ballot measure requiring schools to designate “biological sexes” to sports teams, is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Voters approved the constitutional amendment, known as Initiative Measure 442, which would require public schools, both K-12 and colleges and universities — in addition to any private schools that compete against them — to designate sports teams as either male, female or co-ed/mixed. The measure is projected to pass with nearly 68 percent support, with over 95 percent of the vote tallied by DDHQ.

The initiative would have also blocked transgender girls and women from playing on sports teams that align with their gender identity.

Nebraska passed a law in 2025 requiring public education institutions in the state to designate these teams by sex assigned at birth. Under the statute, women cannot play on sports teams designated for men “unless there is no female team offered or available for such sport for such female student.”

The state’s law also requires students to prove verification of their sex by a physician.

The difference with the ballot measure is that it would largely enshrine those requirements into the state Constitution.

Republicans have heavily leaned into the question of whether transgender people — particularly transgender women or girls — should be allowed to use private facilities or play on sports teams that align with their gender identity. The issue has also divided some Democrats.

Data from the think tank Williams Institute at the University of California, Los Angeles, School of Law estimated in 2025 that there are around 300,000 young individuals — ages 13 to 17 — who identify as transgender in the country in total. A separate dataset also shows roughly 400,000 people aged 18 to 24 years also identify as transgender in the U.S.

articles.title: Winners and losers of the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Democrats pulled off the blue wave of their dreams on Tuesday, winning the House and Senate majorities in a stunning cap to the most expensive midterm election cycle on record. The midterm results are a massive victory for the party, which suffered bruising losses in the last presidential election. It gives Democrats a real chance of…
articles.body:
Democrats pulled off the blue wave of their dreams on Tuesday, winning the House and Senate majorities in a stunning cap to the most expensive midterm election cycle on record.

The midterm results are a massive victory for the party, which suffered bruising losses in the last presidential election. It gives Democrats a real chance of curbing President Trump’s power through the end of his second term.

It was a bleak night for Republicans, from Ohio, where GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy fell to Democrat Amy Acton after a controversial last-ditch ad, to Maine, where five-term incumbent Sen. Susan Collins was toppled by Democrat Troy Jackson.

Results were still rolling in as of 3 a.m. ET, but Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) expected Democrats to win 258 seats in the House and 55 in the Senate — plus a string of flips in governor’s mansions across the country.

Here are the biggest losers and winners of the midterms:

President Trump received a loud repudiation from voters on Tuesday, even though he wasn’t on the ballot.

His party lost its majorities in both chambers of Congress, and by wider-than-expected margins.

It leaves Trump tangling with empowered Democrats for the next two years and will make it tougher for the president to confirm judges and other appointees. Legislative victories will be impossible without working with Democrats.

The last time Trump was president and Democrats held congressional majorities, the president was impeached twice. That’s a real possibility going forward, though one that would hold dangers for both sides.

Presidents typically lose House and Senate seats in a midterm election, but the GOP losses in this case were severe.

Trump’s decisions to mount a war against Iran, which has raised the price of gas and fertilizer, and to engage in a tariff war with Canada both faced blowback. His backing of controversial candidates, most notably Texas state Attorney General Ken Paxton, also backfired.

Trump saw midterm losses coming and pushed redistricting plans across the country in an attempt to protect his congressional majorities.

That ended up backfiring in red states such as Texas and Florida, and it looked likely to leave Democrats with majorities of a size similar to those enjoyed by former President Obama in 2009.

Republicans in the Lone Star State saw one of their worst election cycles, as they lost Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) seat to Democrat James Talarico and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) conceded his reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

The two Democratic victories mark the party’s first statewide wins in Texas in decades.

Tuesday’s results mark the end of Republicans’ statewide dominance in Texas, even after the party redistricted its congressional lines to get a boost in House races.

The blue wave also looked poised to flood through the state Legislature and flip long-red state roles, including the Texas comptroller and Texas railroad commissioner .

Elon Musk also suffered a blow after spending heavily across the country, especially in Texas. On the one hand, Musk’s spending was critical for Republicans as their fundraising advantage served as one bright spot for the party in what was otherwise a challenging midterm environment.

Yet, those dollars were not enough to withstand the seismic political shifts in Texas, which has not elected a Democratic governor since 1990 or a Democratic senator since 1988.

Despite a Trump endorsement and multiple visits from the president and Vice President Vance, Ramaswamy lost the governor’s race in Ohio after running a controversial ad in the campaign’s closing days.

The billionaire biotech entrepreneur funneled millions of his own funds into the 2026 governor’s race, but he came up short against Acton, who’s now on track to become the first Democrat to hold the office in roughly 15 years.

Ramaswamy, who was also backed by term-limited Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R), put $4 million behind an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother calling the Democrat a “liar,” though Acton has described a childhood of abuse, including rape charges against her late stepfather. Acton’s brother Phillip Stearns said their parents lost custody of the two of them after the stepfather was charged by a grand jury, and their mother remained married to their stepfather until his death.

The ad was seen as a last-ditch pitch from Ramaswamy’s team as he trailed in polls, and Tuesday’s results mark a stunning loss for the firebrand Republican in what had been seen as Trump territory.

Sen. Roger Marshall’s (R-Kan.) shock loss to Democrat Adam Hamilton was a blow to Republicans and a reminder that candidate quality still matters, regardless of the state.

While Marshall dealt with the same difficult political climate as other Republicans, he was also hurt by his own missteps as Hamilton became the first Democratic senator to represent Kansas since 1932.

Marshall, an OB-GYN, attracted scrutiny in September after The New York Times reported he had sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical debt. More than 80 patients were arrested for missing their scheduled court appearances, according to the newspaper.

Marshall then cut a rogue ad addressing the issue head-on — an idea some of his staff had reportedly advised against, according to the Times .

In the ad , Marshall disputed the idea that anyone was jailed over the issue while acknowledging that “we occasionally handed some accounts over to a collection agency, just like nearly every private medical practice does.”

“My involvement in any patient’s account ended the minute it was turned over to an outside agency,” he added.

Marshall also faced scrutiny over whether taxpayer dollars were being used for campaign activity, and a bakery accused Marshall’s campaign of failing to pay a bill in 2020. Marshall’s campaign later confirmed it had rectified the unpaid bill.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) put up a strong campaign for a sixth term in the Senate but was swept up in the blue wave that delivered Democrats the upper chamber majority.

A rare Republican to win statewide in blue-leaning Maine, Collins was one of her party’s most vulnerable Senate incumbents.

She stood to benefit from disarray on the Democratic side, as Maine’s initial Senate nominee dropped out amid controversy and party leaders picked Troy Jackson to replace him. She also took pains to keep Trump at arm’s length, criticizing the president’s controversial tariff moves and touting her support for abortion rights.

But Jackson argued that Collins would mean more of the status quo for Mainers, hammering her alignment with Trump and her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.

Ultimately, frustration with Republican-led Washington drove voters to the polls and led to stunning flips across the country — and Collins could not escape the sweep.

She was notably trailing in DDHQ’s polling averages heading into Election Day; Jackson led Collins by 8 points with 83 percent of the vote counted as of 2:50 a.m.

When she first ran for the office in 1996, Collins pledged she would only serve two terms if elected to the Senate. Her loss deprives her of a sixth term that would have made her the longest-serving senator in Maine history.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) came out as the night’s biggest winners as their party flipped both chambers of Congress — and handily so.

A year ago, Democrats were seen as having a fighting chance to flip the House, yet the idea of the party flipping the Senate seemed unthinkable. The initial months of Trump’s second term were also rocky for Schumer, who angered members of his party when he said Democrats would threaten a shutdown over government funding only to later reverse himself.

Senate candidates like Juliana Stratton in Illinois and Hamilton in Kansas said they wouldn’t vote for Schumer as Senate Democratic leader.

And while Schumer angered members of his party for weighing in on several competitive Senate primary contests, his recruits in several of those states ended up winning, delivering the party its majority.

Jeffries will become the first Black House Speaker, and he’ll have a large enough majority that he’ll be able to lose votes on the floor and still pass legislation. It’s a shift from the very narrow majorities with which Speaker Mike Johnson (La.) and the GOP have struggled.

Ossoff’s relatively early race call, which DDHQ made less than half an hour after the polls closed in Georgia at 7 p.m., and his decisive 18-point victory in the battleground state offered an early bright spot for the party.

The Senate GOP once saw Ossoff’s seat as a prime pickup chance and hoped to recruit Gov. Brian Kemp (R) to run for it.

Kemp decided not to run, and the GOP primary became a proxy war between the president and Kemp, with Kemp backing former football coach Derek Dooley while members of Trump’s political orbit worked with Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.).

Republicans sought to show a unified front after Collins won a heated primary runoff, but controversies bogged Collins down, and Ossoff never looked back.

Ossoff’s dominant win is likely to reignite speculation over whether he will run for the White House. The Georgia Democrat vowed that he would finish a second term in the Senate if reelected, though the election night results are likely to encourage more chatter about his prospects.

Other Democrats rumored to have 2028 aspirations or floated as possible candidates also appear on track to have a good night. While redistricting largely backfired for Republicans, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) looks poised to come out on top in the Golden State as his party redrew and flipped several Republican-held seats.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) also enjoyed a good night after one of her top candidates, progressive Abdul El-Sayed, won the Michigan Senate race against Republican Mike Rogers.

Democrats in states across the South achieved some notable upsets, giving the party hope it is building inroads in an area with a growing number of electoral votes.

Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) for Senate while Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in the governor’s race. Pediatrician Annie Andrews pulled off a major upset in South Carolina by defeating Trump-backed Sen. Darline Graham (R), and just more than 2,000 votes separate Scott Colom (D), who is currently in the lead as of 3 a.m. ET, and Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) in the Mississippi race for Senate.

Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.), whose seat was redistricted to heavily favor Republicans this cycle, defeated Alabama state Rep. Rhett Marques (R).

Polls took a lot of heat ahead of Election Day. But the pollsters had a good night, with their surveys pointing to a big Democratic wave looking spot-on.

An eye-popping set of polls from The New York Times/Siena University over the weekend, for example, showed Democratic Senate hopefuls ahead in seven battleground states — Michigan, Texas, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Alaska and Iowa — with mere days to go until the election. As of 3 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Democrats had won in six, with just the Alaska Senate race still uncalled. The Times/Siena poll also showed a tightening race in that state.

Polls in the Trump era have notably overestimated Democratic support in the last three presidential elections, according to analysis from Nate Silver, and experts have been wary that Democrats are more likely to take part in surveys.

That fueled Election Day worries that races would break toward Republicans in margin-of-error races — or worse, add to the history books of major pollster misses.

The numbers bore out on Tuesday, though, as Democrats’ dreamed-of blue wave turned into a blue tsunami.

Democrats flipped four governor’s mansions on Tuesday with a burst of history-making wins.

Acton emerged the victor against Ramaswamy in Ohio, becoming the first Democrat elected to the office in roughly 15 years and the first woman elected as governor in Buckeye State history.

In Texas, Hinojosa joined Talarico as the first Democrats to win statewide in decades. She’ll also be the first Latina sworn in as governor in the Lone Star State, and just the second woman to serve that role.

In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn to become the first Democratic Iowa governor in 20 years.

And Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms’s flip against Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia makes her the first Black woman elected governor in the country.

As of 3 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Democrats were also favored to flip the Alaska governor’s office, which had yet to be called. They were also on track to hold Kansas, while Republican-held Nevada was a toss-up.

Republicans, on the other hand, didn’t flip any blue-held governor’s offices into their column.

The results leave Democratic governors to lead in traditionally red states, promising to dramatically reshape their states’ politics and the national landscape through the end of Trump’s second term.

articles.title: Idaho rejects ballot measure adding abortion access protection
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would legalize abortion access up until fetal viability in Idaho, reversing the state’s current ban, is projected to fail, according to Decision Desk HQ. Voters rejected the ballot measure, which sought to establish protections around reproductive access in the Gem State up to viability, around 23 to 24 weeks, when the…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would legalize abortion access up until fetal viability in Idaho, reversing the state’s current ban, is projected to fail, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Voters rejected the ballot measure, which sought to establish protections around reproductive access in the Gem State up to viability, around 23 to 24 weeks, when the fetus is likely to survive outside the womb. Fifty-six percent of voters rejected the measure with over 95 percent of the vote reported as of early Wednesday.

The measure would have carved out an exemption for cases of medical emergency for any abortions performed after that period.

It also would have given people the right to make decisions around other aspects of reproductive care, including contraception and fertility treatment.

If approved, the initiative would repeal the state’s standing abortion restrictions , which make it a crime for physicians to perform the procedure except in very narrow cases pertaining to the life of the mother or instances of reported rape or incest.

The Supreme Court’s landmark decision in 2022 to overturn Roe v. Wade ushered in a patchwork of state laws that varied in how they regulated abortion access.

Democrats and reproductive groups have leaned into the issue , including the right to have an abortion, as a way of reversing the high court’s decision across the country — while also using it as a tool to gin up enthusiasm among their bases amid the election cycle.

Several states, including Missouri, Nevada and Virginia, are also teeing up ballot measures around reproductive access this fall.

articles.title: Arizona approves ballot measure designating sexes to sports teams
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would further restrict transgender people from competing on sports teams or using private spaces like locker rooms that align with their gender identity is projected to pass in Arizona, according to Decision Desk HQ. Voters approved the ballot measure, otherwise known as Proposition 318, which requires both private and public schools…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would further restrict transgender people from competing on sports teams or using private spaces like locker rooms that align with their gender identity is projected to pass in Arizona, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Voters approved the ballot measure, otherwise known as Proposition 318, which requires both private and public schools in addition to athletic associations to designate sports teams as male, female or co-ed based on “biological sex” and “to prevent males from joining female teams,” referring to transgender women playing in sports that align with their gender identity.

Nearly 58 percent of voters backed the proposition, with 69 percent of the vote reported early Wednesday morning.

The effort would also bar schools from allowing transgender people to use private spaces that don’t align with their sex assigned at birth, defining the word “sex” as “as an individual’s biological status as male or female as recorded at birth on an original birth certificate.”

The measure notes that currently only public schools and their competing rivals are subject to rules around sex designations of sports teams.

Republicans have heavily leaned into issues around whether transgender people can use private facilities or play on sports teams that align with their gender identity in recent years, and the issues have divided some Democrats.

GOP lawmakers have specifically focused on transgender girls and women looking to play in girls’ and women’s sports leagues.

The Williams Institute at the University of California, Los Angeles School of Law estimated in 2025 that there around 300,000 young individuals — ages 13 to 17 — who identify as transgender in the country in total. Separately, roughly 400,000 people aged 18 to 24 years old identify this way.

articles.title: Yarbrough wins Texas House election for redistricted Julie Johnson seat
articles.summary: Texas Republican House candidate Jace Yarbrough is projected to win the open seat to lead the state’s redistricted 32nd District and replace Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas), per Decision Desk HQ. The attorney defeated Richardson City Council member Dan Barrios (D) in the district redrawn to favor Republicans last year. Johnson opted to run in the…
articles.body:
Texas Republican House candidate Jace Yarbrough is projected to win the open seat to lead the state’s redistricted 32nd District and replace Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas), per Decision Desk HQ.

The attorney defeated Richardson City Council member Dan Barrios (D) in the district redrawn to favor Republicans last year. Johnson opted to run in the nearby 33rd District but lost to former Rep. Colin Allred (D-Texas) in the primary.

Yarbrough notched support from several prominent Republicans, including President Trump and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R). Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, who previously supported Trump and has ties with Vice President Vance, sent two $3,500 donations to Yarbrough’s campaign in December 2025, one for the primary and one for the general election, according to Federal Election Commission filings .

Yarbrough faced a GOP runoff against businessman Ryan Binkley, but Binkley withdrew in March after the initial primary, where Yarbrough finished in first place with more than 48.9 percent of the vote. Binkley credited Yarbrough for running a “disciplined campaign” at the time and expressed excitement to see how Yarbrough would do in the House.

In February, Yarbrough took part in a forum hosted by conservative news site The Dallas Express, where he expressed views that critics have condemned as extremist. He called for repealing the 1965 Hart-Celler Act, which put an end to race-based immigration quotas, and claimed that “hordes of Islamic immigrants” came to the U.S. to “set up” Sharia law.

“The kind of good government that I want to offer, that you and I agree with –– they call it bigoted and backward and oppressive and Nazi-ish,” he said at the forum. “I am past trying to placate that in any way, shape or form.”

The Stanford Law School graduate served as the president of his alma mater’s chapter of the Federalist Society . He later served in the U.S. Air Force and remains active in the Air Force Reserve.
