articles.title: Alabama voters approve school prayer, Pledge of Allegiance amendment
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would amend the Alabama Constitution to essentially require the Pledge of Allegiance in public schools in addition to allowing “student-initiated and student-led prayer” is projected to be approved by voters, according to Decision Desk HQ. Voters in the Cotton State passed the constitutional amendment, known as Alabama Statewide Amendment 3, which…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would amend the Alabama Constitution to essentially require the Pledge of Allegiance in public schools in addition to allowing “student-initiated and student-led prayer” is projected to be approved by voters, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Voters in the Cotton State passed the constitutional amendment, known as Alabama Statewide Amendment 3 , which would require local school boards “to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to conduct The Pledge of Allegiance to the United States flag” daily in addition to adopting policies allowing student-initiated, student-led prayer.

Students would still be allowed to opt out of reciting the pledge or participating in student-led prayer. The ballot measure needed more than half of the vote to pass.

The measure passed early Wednesday with 63 percent of the vote, according to DDHQ.

Alabama already has a law on the books that directs schools to say the pledge, though students are allowed to sit it out. School prayer is also covered in the state.

The difference here is that this requirement would be included in the state constitution and would allow policies around student-initiated prayer.

Battles around religious freedom and public education have played out in recent years, including earlier this year, when a federal appellate court ultimately allowed Louisiana to enforce a law mandating the Ten Commandments be displayed in public schools.

articles.title: The 2028 presidential race starts now. These 6 Democrats just had a great night
articles.summary: The 2028 presidential race effectively begins now, and Tuesday’s midterms elections offered an early snapshot of the political strength of the Democratic Party’s potential White House contenders. For some would-be candidates, the results strengthened their political standing and bolstered their case for becoming the party’s next standard-bearer. Here’s a look at who emerged from election night…
articles.body:
The 2028 presidential race effectively begins now, and Tuesday’s midterms elections offered an early snapshot of the political strength of the Democratic Party’s potential White House contenders.

For some would-be candidates, the results strengthened their political standing and bolstered their case for becoming the party’s next standard-bearer.

Here’s a look at who emerged from election night with the most political capital.

The Georgia senator faced a consequential test in a state President Trump carried two years ago. And he didn’t just perform well, he exceeded expectations. Exit polling showed he grew his numbers with independent voters.

Even before he defeated his GOP opponent, Rep. Mike Collins, with 63 percent of the vote to the Republican’s 37 percent, he was already being compared by some to a previous successful, young Democratic senator who moved to the White House.

“Democrats pin hopes on the new Obama,” a headline from The Telegraph ran hours before Ossoff’s victory.

The big question with Ossoff is whether he will run for the presidency.

Ossoff recently pledged that he would serve out his full six-year term in the Senate, and he said he has no interest in running for president.

That sounds like something a Senate candidate with presidential aspirations is supposed to say on the reelection trail, but people in Ossoff’s orbit say it’s not just political speak and that the senator truly does not want to run.

But Democratic donors and strategists say he could be pushed to change his mind.

Democratic strategist Steve Schale said Ossoff’s win will rocket him to the top of many Democrats’ lists, and he said the chattering class of donors and other operatives could pull him in.

“There’s so much room in the field for him right now,” he said.

The California governor made his state’s redistricting effort the centerpiece of his political strategy last year, and it paid dividends on Tuesday night.

While some Republican redistricting efforts failed to yield major gains — in Florida, for example — Newsom will be able to point to his success in helping Democrats gain seats as the vote count trickles in to the Golden State.

The results also highlight Newsom’s massive political network, which helped boost his redistricting efforts. Even before he leaves the governor’s mansion in January, he can tout these efforts as something tangible.

“He walked the walk,” one Democratic mega-donor said. “He didn’t just talk the talk.”

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) won reelection as expected Tuesday night, but the race she was paying attention to was not her own but instead a Senate race in Michigan.

Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed was projected as the winner early Wednesday by The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ, and it’s a win that is a boon to Ocasio-Cortez and her presidential prospects.

Ocasio-Cortez invested in a big way in El-Sayed’s campaign, donating $1 million in the race and campaigning alongside him. His victory in a state Trump carried in 2024 gives Ocasio-Cortez and other progressives a new line that they can win anywhere — even in battleground states — something she has told Democrats privately in recent days.

Ocasio-Cortez has been weighing her options for 2028 — including a possible presidential campaign or a Senate bid in New York. But some Democratic strategists say El-Sayed’s win may push her over the edge.

The former Transportation secretary wasn’t on the ballot on Tuesday, but he spent much of the midterm cycle crisscrossing the country and campaigning for Democratic candidates, more than many of his potential rivals.

He made more than 17 public campaign stops since Labor Day, according to National Journal.

Buttigieg, who now resides in Michigan, also helped raise money for candidates and state parties, building the foundation of contacts he would need to help launch a campaign.

On election night, Buttigieg, in a CNN appearance, was already trying to frame an economic argument, saying that Democrats needed to “come out of the gate quickly” with a plan “that makes Americans better off.”

The Pennsylvania governor cruised to a decisive victory in the swing state of Pennsylvania against Republican Stacy Garrity, in a race that was called as soon as polls closed.

Shapiro’s coattails were also effective, as a number of Pennsylvania Democrats won victories in House races, helping the party take the House majority by a comfortable margin.

The governor invested $10 million of his campaign war chest in an effort that helped flip four Republican-held congressional seats, and it helped Democrats win control of the state Legislature.

“He’s been really underrated in recent months, mostly because he had to focus on winning his race, but I think he comes out of this in a super strong position if he tries to run for president,” one Democratic consultant said.

Tuesday’s results give Shapiro an argument to make on the campaign trail: Not only can he win in a key state, but he’s been helpful to other Democrats in his state as well.

The Kentucky governor wasn’t on the ballot Tuesday, but he heavily benefited from the results.

As chair of the Democratic Governors Association, Beshear — who was elected twice in ruby-red Kentucky — helped to usher in a string of Democratic gubernatorial wins, including in Republican-held states like Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Texas.

“This was a huge night for him,” the Democratic donor said. “Governors — particularly moderate governors — had major wins, and Beshear needs to get some credit for it.”

articles.title: ‘LAWYER UP’: Democrats, Republicans waste no time in setting social media ablaze after midterm sweep
articles.summary: Sen. Ron Wyden's one-word post — "Subpoenas" — set the tone as Democrats celebrated reclaiming both the House and Senate in 2026 midterms.
articles.body: Explosive reactions to the 2026 midterm elections quickly spread online as it became clear that Democrats had routed Republicans in key contests, reclaiming control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate early Wednesday morning. While Republicans quickly looked for a source of blame, jubilant Democratic reactions ranged from calling the moment the end of Trump’s MAGA movement to aggressive predictions of what the party could accomplish with their newfound majorities. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., summed up his vision for Senate committees in only one word. "Subpoenas," Wyden said in a post on X. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH Democrats like Wyden have long promised to summon members of the current administration, former officials and business leaders before lawmakers for questioning if they captured a majority. In the House, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., echoed Wyden’s thinking with a brief post of his own. "LAWYER UP," Garcia wrote. Still other voices in the Democratic Party expressed the magnitude of the victory in more colorful terms. "WE’RE GONNA PUT YOUR ASS IN JAIL EVERYONE GET MORE WORK RIGHT NOW !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!" Hasan Piker, a progressive streamer and socialist, said in a post to X. Piker, who aligned himself closely with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party in the 2026 midterms, supported several candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). He also campaigned with Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, who won his race against Mike Rogers, a former congressman. "GOD IS NONBINARY NOW MFS!!! IT'S LAW!!!" he wrote in another post, referring to James Talarico’s Senate victory in Texas over Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico received widespread criticism from Republicans for past comments where he described God as "nonbinary" — an instance Republicans used to characterize Talarico as too progressive to represent a Republican-leaning state like Texas. DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS After Fox News Decision Desk projected victories by Talarico and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa over Gov. Greg Abbott, other progressives cast the wins as a symbol of Democratic momentum. "TEXAS IS BLUE. THIS IS HISTORY," Dean Withers, another progressive political commentator, wrote in a post to social media. "MAGA IS DEAD. THEY’RE F---ING DEAD. WOKE HAS NEVER BEEN MORE BACK," he added. On the other side of the aisle, Republicans and conservatives took to social media to vent frustrations and begin identifying where they thought the party had lost traction with the public. To Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who lost a primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger, the midterm outcome boiled down to a set of unfulfilled promises: broken pledges to stay out of foreign conflicts and commitments to bring transparency around Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced businessman who had died in prison while awaiting trial. "Tonight’s outcome isn’t about placing faith in Democrats or socialist principles; it’s about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises. All Republicans had to do was: 1. put Americans First 2. not start another war 3. prosecute sex traffickers," Massie wrote. Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former congresswoman who resigned her seat earlier this year over disagreements with the administration, delivered a similar message. "Trump’s biggest betrayal to the American people isn’t what he failed to do. It’s what he promised NOT to do… and did it anyway," Greene wrote in a post to X. "We gave President Trump our support, we gave him our money, we gave him our vote and gave him our time and we got behind him publicly, and he didn’t deliver," she added. Conservative political commentator Matt Walsh offered similar criticisms of Trump, focusing on the U.S. conflict with Iran. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES "The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least. A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles," Walsh said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There’s no way to soft-pedal this. It’s a political catastrophe of historic proportions. The Republican Party needs all new leadership. None should be spared from blame, starting at the top," Walsh added in a separate post.

articles.title: New York, Oregon laws could make the Supreme Court defend its Janus ruling
articles.summary: In 2018, the U.S. Supreme Court handed public-sector unions a well-deserved rebuke in Janus v. AFSCME. The justices affirmed that government employees cannot be compelled to financially support a union as a condition of employment. Eight years later, the question is whether the court is willing to defend the principle it enunciated. So far, it…
articles.body:
In 2018, the U.S. Supreme Court handed public-sector unions a well-deserved rebuke in Janus v. AFSCME. The justices affirmed that government employees cannot be compelled to financially support a union as a condition of employment.

Eight years later, the question is whether the court is willing to defend the principle it enunciated. So far, it has not. But two ongoing lawsuits might just be egregious enough to change that.

Oregon and New York recently enacted remarkably similar laws. On their face, they claim their intention is to prevent organizations from fraudulently impersonating labor unions, which sounds reasonable enough. Fraud is already illegal, and nobody has a constitutional right to deceive workers.

But these laws actually have a much more specific target: The Freedom Foundation, my own national watchdog organization, whose mission is to inform government employees of their right to decline union membership and dues — and when necessary, to help them exercise it, since unions often make it as difficult as they can.

That distinction matters. Oregon’s law, passed last year, prohibits falsely impersonating a union representative and provides statutory damages of $6,250 per incident. In response, the Freedom Foundation filed a lawsuit challenging the measure, arguing that its communications are identified and that the law merely chills constitutionally protected speech. After a federal district court dismissed the case, the organization appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

New York followed this past spring with Civil Service Law Section 216. The statute authorizes Attorney General Letitia James to act when she believes someone has engaged — or is “about to engage” — in prohibited communications. Violations can result in fines of $1,000 per incident.

The Freedom Foundation sued New York on Sept. 28.

The constitutional problem isn’t merely what happens when someone is prosecuted. It is what happens before. At no point in testimony on behalf of either bill did union backers even attempt to present evidence that the Freedom Foundation has tried to mislead anyone. But under the laws they managed to pass, the organization must now consider whether a mailing, advertisement or email could later be characterized as a “material omission,” “misrepresentation” or “other deception” by a partisan attorney general, union lawyer or judge.

That is how speech gets chilled. You don’t necessarily need to censor someone outright when you can make speaking prohibitively risky.

Which brings us back to Janus. Since 2018, public-sector unions and their political allies have developed a variety of mechanisms to it more difficult to opt out of union membership. In response, the Freedom Foundation has represented dozens of workers trying to cut ties with their unions. We have repeatedly asked the Supreme Court to intervene in post-Janus disputes, including cases involving restrictions on resigning union membership and unions refusing to accept opt-out paperwork.

The court has ignored every appeal, and that restraint has had consequences. When the Supreme Court stubbornly refuses to police its own boundaries, those regulated by the decision inevitably begin testing how far they can go. The laws passed in Oregon and New York represent the logical next step.

In addition to making it needlessly difficult for employees to exercise their rights, union allies are now trying to suppress the information necessary for those same employees to make that choice by rendering it legally hazardous for outside organizations to tell them their rights.

To be clear, neither Janus nor the First Amendment addresses fraud. They don’t need to. If an organization actually does impersonate a union, deliberately deceives workers and causes harm, states have legitimate tools for dealing with that.

But these state governments are using the threat of potential fraud allegations as a convenient excuse to muzzle dissent. Public officials should not be empowered to threaten speakers with potentially enormous penalties based on vague standards whose application rests largely on the political sympathies of those enforcing them.

That is why these cases have relevance that goes far beyond the Freedom Foundation.

Our organization has now challenged both statutes in federal court. Eventually, one or both cases could reach the Supreme Court. If and when they do, the justices should finally seize the opportunity to send an unambiguous message to government employee unions.

For eight years, the Supreme Court has largely watched from the sidelines while unions and sympathetic lawmakers probed the limits of Janus. Enough is enough. A constitutional right that governments can burden, obstruct or frighten people out of exercising is no right at all.

The justices drew a line in the sand with Janus in 2018. If Oregon or New York’s law reaches their doorstep, they should finally make clear that line is carved in stone.

Jeff Rhodes is vice president of news and information at the Freedom Foundation.

articles.body:
Mississippi’s Senate race remained too close to call early Wednesday, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom holding a razor-thin lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) of less than 1 percentage point.

With nearly all ballots counted, Colom led Hyde-Smith by a little more than 2,000 votes — 461,370 to 459,201 — as of early Wednesday morning, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The contest has put the reliably red state in the national spotlight as Democrats celebrate massive victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections, winning control of both chambers of Congress and flipping several Republican-held Senate seats.

A victory for Colom, a district attorney in the Magnolia State, would mark the eighth Senate seat Democrats have flipped this election cycle and a stunning political shift in Mississippi, which President Trump won by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.

The race drew increasing attention in the closing days of the campaign as Democrats saw an opportunity to unseat Hyde-Smith, who was widely viewed as weak on the campaign trail, despite the state’s strong GOP lean.

Colom’s showing in the contest comes amid a wave of blue victories in states considered to be Republican strongholds, including Kansas , where Adam Hamilton defeated Sen. Roger Marshall (R), and South Carolina , where Annie Andrews ousted Sen. Darline Graham (R).

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Trump-backed state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), delivering the party its first Senate victory in the Lone Star State in nearly four decades.

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982, when former Sen. John Stennis won his final term.

articles.title: El-Sayed: ‘Delicious irony’ that ‘habibi’ Vance ‘constitutionally obligated’ to swear him in
articles.summary: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) taunted President Trump and Vice President Vance in his victory speech early Wednesday after the two Republicans spent months attacking him on the campaign trail. El-Sayed, who defeated Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s closely watched Senate race, joked about the prospect of Vance swearing him in to office in…
articles.body:
Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) taunted President Trump and Vice President Vance in his victory speech early Wednesday after the two Republicans spent months attacking him on the campaign trail.

El-Sayed, who defeated Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s closely watched Senate race, joked about the prospect of Vance swearing him in to office in January, calling it a moment of “delicious irony” after Vance’s public personal jabs .

“JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed said in a speech to supporters in Detroit, using an Arabic term of affection.

“Wolverines 1, Buckeyes 0,” he added, referencing the rivalry between the University of Michigan and Ohio State University, Vance’s alma mater.

The Democrat then turned his attention to Trump, who repeatedly mocked El-Sayed’s name and attacked his Muslim faith during the campaign.

“Donald, I know you struggle with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you can go on and call me senator,” El-Sayed said.

The remarks marked a victory lap for El-Sayed, who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate after a bruising campaign in which his religion and progressive positions drew fierce opposition from Republicans.

Vance previously described El-Sayed as “very, very evil,” while Trump has repeatedly referred to the Democrat as a “jihadist” and a “communist.” Republicans also alleged that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed has denied.

The president escalated his attacks in the final hours before Election Day, claiming in a Truth Social post early Tuesday morning that El-Sayed “Hates Jews and Hates Blacks.”

At a rally in South Carolina, Trump told the crowd: “If you’re Black or if you’re Jewish, and if you vote for Abdul, you’re crazy.”

El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, will succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.), keeping the seat in Democratic hands after one of the most contentious Senate contests of the midterm cycle.

articles.title: GOP crushed in blue landslide
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Democrats take control of House, Senate ▪ Elected candidates deliver historic firsts ▪ Alaska results could take weeks ▪ Mississippi Senate down to the wire Democrats’ wildest dreams came true Tuesday night as they swept battlegrounds and made stunning inroads into red territory on their way to clear majorities in both…
articles.body:
▪ Democrats take control of House, Senate

▪ Elected candidates deliver historic firsts

Democrats’ wildest dreams came true Tuesday night as they swept battlegrounds and made stunning inroads into red territory on their way to clear majorities in both the House and Senate.

The party won in essentially everywhere they had their eye on and then some, with the blue wave only growing stronger as more returns came in.

In the Senate races , the wave swept South Carolina, Kansas, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Michigan and Maine into the blue column, with Alaska and Mississippi still too close to call this morning. Democrats are on track to win 54 to 56 seats.

Over in the House, Democrats are positioned to pull off wins that would have seemed inconceivable, putting them on the path to win some 255 seats.

Some of the most closely watched races weren’t close.

After a contentious race that cost at least half a billion dollars, Democrat James Talarico cruised to victory over Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton . He’s ahead by nearly 12 points, as of the latest vote count.

Talarico is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since 1988.

The Democratic wave in the Lone Star State was big enough to even sink three-term Gov. Greg Abbott (R), the longest-serving governor in the country. He conceded to state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D), trailing by more than 7 points.

Perhaps even more stunning was Democrat Adam Hamilton ‘s defeat of Sen. Roger Marshall in ruby-red Kansas, a state that has not had a Democratic senator since the 1930s. The megachurch pastor is on track to win by almost 5 points, as of the latest tally.

The real shocker came in South Carolina, as President Trump ‘s hand-picked candidate, Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), lost in a major upset to Democrat Annie Andrews . Graham was elevated to the role to succeed her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), after the staunch Trump ally’s sudden death this summer.

One of the earliest signs of the night’s trajectory came in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, home to Rep. Victoria Spartz (R), where Trump won by 22 points and Spartz by 18 in 2024. Democrat J.D. Ford was up by more than 3 points with most votes counted in the suburban Indianapolis district.

In what would be one of the most high-profile defeats of the night, Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), the chair of House Republicans’ campaign arm, is trailing by more than 2 points with more than 95 percent of the vote counted.

Rep. Jeff Van Drew , a former Democrat-turned-Republican who has represented a comfortably conservative area of New Jersey for years, conceded defeat to Democrat Zack Mullock .

Rep. Ann Wager (R-Mo.) lost a seat she’s held for more than a decade in the St. Louis suburbs.

Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie (D) ousted GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick , one of four vulnerable House Republicans in Pennsylvania who won’t be returning to Congress in January.

The GOP’s efforts to pad its conference through mid-decade redistricting largely fell flat, too. No incumbent Democrat seeking reelection lost, even in districts that were shifted to become heavily more conservative.

That seems likely to include Rep. Darren Soto (D-Fla.), who was facing the biggest challenge of any Democrat seeking reelection. Despite running in a district that would have voted for Trump by 17 points in 2024, Soto is on track to squeak out a win. Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.), who was also facing a tough challenge, held on comfortably in a much more conservative area of Alabama.

The Democratic majorities are shaping up to be the largest for either party in both chambers since the start of former President Obama ‘s administration.

“There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Tuesday night. “Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must deliver.”

“MAGA extremists are on the run from sea to shining sea,” said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), who is likely to be the next Speaker of the House.

Texas-based Republican strategist Brendan Steinhauser dubbed the night an “utter disaster” in a text message, along with a gif of the Titanic sinking.

The Hill Insiders can read more from Julia Manchester and Helen Huiskes about how the blue wave broke Trump’s midterm map.

▪ The Hill : Winners and losers of the 2026 midterms.

▪ The Hill : Five takeaways on a midterm rout for Democrats.

▪ The Hill : Trump congratulates Democrats after midterm romp.

Democrats are projected to gain a majority of governorships for the first time since 2006. They owe that to key wins in hotly contested races in multiple states, including Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. They’re also currently winning gubernatorial races in Alaska, Kansas and Nevada.

Abortion rights advocates notched a few big wins in the night, as voters approved measures to add protections to state constitutions in Virginia and Nevada . Voters also rejected a measure that would have overturned protections in Missouri. One state where efforts fell short was Idaho , where voters rejected a measure to overturn the abortion ban in the state.

Expect a big shift in multiple state governments. Democrats are on track to win governing trifectas in at least Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Nevada. Some of these states haven’t had unified Democratic government in years. New trifectas are also possible in both Arizona and Alaska.

Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms waves to supporters at an election night event, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Brynn Anderson)

BREAKING BARRIERS : Last night’s historic outcomes extended beyond just Democrats’ stunning sweep of several deep-red states. Voters also elected candidates whose victories broke barriers in Senate, House and governors’ races across the country.

Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) became the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.

Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) became the first Black person elected governor of Florida. He is also the first Black Republican elected governor of a U.S. state.

Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland (D) became the first Native American woman elected governor of a U.S. state.

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) is the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate.

Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) will be the state’s first Latina governor.

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (D) became the first Black governor elected in Wisconsin.

Democrat Annie Andrews became the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate in South Carolina.

Tennessee, Minnesota and Georgia are each poised to elect their first female governor.

▪ Fox News : Trump-backed Donalds to make history as Florida’s first Black governor.

▪ The Associated Press : Midterms bringing in wave of historic firsts.

CUT OFF: Trump started Tuesday with big news. He said he reached a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that would cut off the bulk of U.S. foreign aid to Israel at the end of the year.

The president made the announcement just as polls were opening yesterday, but he said the two leaders struck the agreement “months ago.” Trump portrayed the shift in foreign policy as a political move, pointing to Democrats like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan who criticize Israel on the campaign trail.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It’s a bad talking point,” Trump said in an interview on Fox News’s “Fox & Friends.”

But Trump also suggested Israel no longer needs the aid, while calling the country “a great ally” and saying the U.S. would still “help” Israel if the country needs it.

▪ The Hill : Marjorie Taylor Greene says aid cuts show ‘how bad the polling is.’

ON AGAIN OFF AGAIN : A federal appeals court ruled Tuesday to again lift a block on the Trump administration attempting to coerce election workers into setting aside ballots suspected to have been cast by noncitizens.

The ruling reinstates an earlier order from a divided appeals court panel. The Justice Department (DOJ) had been appealing a lower judge’s injunction blocking the administration from threatening state and local officials with criminal prosecution if they didn’t comply with its demands.

The DOJ sent letters last week to California and Washington, requesting they check voter rolls for potential ineligible voters and sequester those ballots until citizenship status can be verified.

Two labor unions and political interest groups sued, accusing the administration of unlawfully trying to interfere with the midterms, arguing it could disenfranchise voters.

The Supreme Court rejected the administration’s emergency request to segregate the California ballots on Monday.

▪ The Hill : Election monitors deployed to every state for first time.

▪ The Associated Press : Judge complicates construction timeline on arch.

FAVORING EXEMPTION : The Supreme Court’s conservative majority appears to be leaning in favor of Catholic preschools seeking an exemption from Colorado’s requirement that they admit the children of same-sex couples.

Colorado funds 15 hours of universal pre-K per week for each eligible student, but participating schools must agree to provide families an “equal opportunity” to enroll regardless of certain criteria, including sexual orientation and gender identity. The Archdiocese of Denver, a group of Catholic parishes and two parents challenged the antidiscrimination provision under First Amendment grounds.

Multiple conservative justices pressed the state for evidence that same-sex couples have been turned away from a preschool.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh suggested the case could be a “win-win” if Colorado backs out, noting that more than 2,000 eligible preschools are available but only a few dozen Catholic schools.

▪ amNY : NYPD argues against court overturning assault weapons ban.

▪ MS NOW : Court sends Trump a midterms message with California order.

The president has no public events scheduled.

Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and Democratic Senate hopeful former Rep. Mary Peltola. (AP Photo/Becky Bohrer)

THE LAST FRONTIER : Alaska’s election results remain unclear as of this morning, with polls only closing at 1 a.m. EST today.

As of the latest vote count, Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) narrowly leads former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) by less than 1 point. About two-thirds of the vote has been counted. The other Dan Sullivan has about 1.6 percent of votes so far.

Neither leading candidate currently holds a majority, so additional rounds of the state’s ranked choice voting system may be needed to determine a winner.

State officials have said it could be another two weeks before a final result is announced, since absentee ballots can arrive through Nov. 18. The ranked-choice tabulation is also scheduled for that day.

The race has garnered outsized attention in recent days, largely spurred on by The New York Times reporting last week that Dan J. Sullivan , who is unrelated to the sitting senator, was recruited by operatives linked to national Democrats and Peltola’s campaign to boost her chances. Peltola and Democratic officials have denied involvement in the scheme.

The practice is not illegal according to state law, and the Times report did not allege any criminal wrongdoing, but there are several ongoing investigations into the scheme. The tight margin will likely bolster will likely encourage GOP efforts to contest the results if Peltola pulls it out.

The incumbent senator’s campaign and the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) have organized a “recount fund,” according to a Federal Election Commission filing yesterday.

“The NRSC is committed to ensuring every vote is counted fairly and accurately, in each and every state, and we will be ready for all contingencies, including recounts, should they be necessary,” NRSC spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez said.

The Justice Department also sent letters to 20 Democrats informing them they are being looked at as part of an investigation into ballot-stacking in Alaska, the Times reported yesterday. The DOJ officials reportedly told recipients to preserve records related to the effort to elect a candidate that shares a name with the incumbent senator.

▪ Alaska Public Media : Alaska counts ballots slowly. Here’s what to expect.

▪ The Associated Press : Alaska voters roiled in final days by litigation, new allegations.

Mississippi Sen. Cyndi Hyde-Smith (R) and Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom. (AP Photo/Sarah Warnock/Jeff Roberson)

DOWN TO THE WIRE : Another possible major upset may be brewing as just a few dozen votes separate the candidates in Mississippi’s Senate race.

Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) by 43 votes with almost all ballots tallied.

That margin is close enough that almost regardless of how the last remaining votes go, a recount seems all but certain. That would take time, and Hyde-Smith may ultimately hang on.

But the fact that the state may flip is just as eye-popping as what happened in nearby South Carolina.

Mississippi hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since the 1980s. This year’s race stayed largely under the radar as Democrats focused on flipping other states seen as more realistically attainable.

But the party began investing in the Magnolia State in the race’s final weeks, spending more than $1 million on an ad campaign targeting Hyde-Smith. Polling from a few Democratic-leaning pollsters showed the race within the margin of error but still with the incumbent ahead.

Now the race seems like it could go either way, possibly extending Democratic success in the deep south.

▪ CNBC : What Trump losing Congress means for Iran, Ukraine.

How Trump and Democrats can navigate divided government , The Washington Post editorial board writes .

Republican reckoning: Accountability finally comes for Trump, Max Burns writes in The Hill.

Various guns are displayed at a store. (AP Photo/Robert F. Bukaty, File)

And finally … An unusual measure was on the ballot in Idaho as voters cast ballots to choose an official state gun in observance of the U.S. semiquincentennial.

The measure is nonbinding, but the state legislature could make it permanent through legislation. Among six choices, the Winchester Model 1873, known as the “Gun that Won the West,” is leading with just more than 31 percent of the vote.

The Winchester Model 1894 follows in second with about 25 percent.

The Idaho state House pointed to a deep history of firearms in both the U.S. and Idaho in bringing the question to the ballot, from armed militias during the Revolutionary War to pioneers using rifles to hunt for food.

articles.title: Thune: Republicans ‘will not stand idly by’ under Democratic majority
articles.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) declared early Wednesday morning that Republicans “will not stand idly by” as Democrats try to reverse the actions of President Trump’s first two years in office by raising taxes or restoring spending cuts to popular programs. And Thune expressed his gratitude that Trump will still be in office over…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) declared early Wednesday morning that Republicans “will not stand idly by” as Democrats try to reverse the actions of President Trump’s first two years in office by raising taxes or restoring spending cuts to popular programs.

And Thune expressed his gratitude that Trump will still be in office over the next two years to veto any legislation passed by a Democratic-controlled Senate and House.

“As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done. Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism,” the senator posted to the social platform X .

“We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream,” he added.

Senate Democrats, led by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), will make renewing the expanded Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies, which expired at the beginning of the year, a top priority in 2027.

They will also seek to unwind the big corporate tax cuts and cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program enacted in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act .

Schumer told reporters on election night that Democrats will also prioritize addressing the affordability crisis in America and investigating “corruption” in the Trump administration.

He noted the new Democratic majorities’ “number one focus has to be producing for the American people in terms of their number one need: the high costs that Trump has imposed on them.”

The second priority would be to “go after the corruption,” the New York Democrat added.

“This is the most corrupt administration in American history,” he said.

Thune also defended Trump’s and Senate Republicans’ records since the 2024 election.

“Over the last two years, Senate Republicans have put up a strong record of accomplishment that’s created safer streets, more money in Americans’ pockets, and new opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead,” he continued in the post.

“After fighting Democrat obstruction at every turn, we prevented the largest tax hike in American history, secured our border in an unprecedented way, confirmed the president’s Cabinet at the fastest pace in two decades, and put strong conservative judges on benches across the country faster than we have since the Reagan administration,” the GOP leader argued.

articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth faces “a reckoning” in the post-election lame-duck Congress and questioned whether President Trump will be able to get the Pentagon funded if Hegseth remains in his job.

“Hegseth has a reckoning,” Tillis told CBS News . “He is one of the reasons why we don’t have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need.

“I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he’s the best person to bring those needs to Congress. If he wants something done before the end of this Congress, which is only 60 days away.”

Democrats have threatened to block the $70 billion in emergency defense funding the Trump administration requested of Congress in June as well as the annual Defense appropriations bill, to fund the Pentagon through fiscal 2027, while the nation is still embroiled in a military conflict with Iran.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told The Hill in September that Hegseth’s departure would help Democratic and Republican lawmakers reach bipartisan deals on defense matters.

Hegseth could face an impeachment vote in the House later this month or in December.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) has warned he will push for a vote on articles of impeachment against Hegseth when Congress reconvenes in Washington next week.

Tillis, who cast the pivotal vote to confirm Hegseth in January 2025, now says that vote is the “biggest regret of my career.”

The North Carolina senator has emerged as a forceful critic of the Pentagon chief and has often criticized him for ousting senior and experienced military leaders at the Defense Department and often disregarding their advice.

He urged Trump to fire Hegseth last month.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” Tillis posted on the social platform X last month.

“I urge the president to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” he said.

articles.title: Are Florida Democrats at a crossroads after Nixon’s run?
articles.summary: JACKSONVILLE — Afterlosing Tuesday’s election to Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, Democrat Angie Nixon was still entirely in campaign mode.
articles.body:
JACKSONVILLE — After losing Tuesday's election to Republican Sen. Ashley Moody , Democrat Angie Nixon was still entirely in campaign mode.

"We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over, and I need y'all to stay in this fight," Nixon told a packed crowd decked out in pink in a Jacksonville warehouse. "2028 is around the corner, so Ashley Moody, you better get it right cause we're coming for you."

Her final words to the room: "Let's go win, y'all!" Then Nixon started dancing.

The disappointment before she had taken the stage was palpable: Supporters had been calling voters up until the final moments before polls closed, still hoping to eke out a long-shot win against the Florida Republican Party's machine.

But Nixon — who mobilized long-ignored voters and drew thousands to rallies — turned the energy around, all but promising another run for the U.S. Senate in two years when Moody is back on the ballot. It wasn't long before she had the room chanting "2028."

Supporters say Nixon modeled how an unapologetic progressive candidate can drive out voters in Florida, and Democrats across the ideological spectrum agree that her candidacy was a tide that raised other Democrats.

Her race was "a mandate from the people in the state of Florida showing that they're long overdue for the leadership from the people that are true progressives and care about the people," said Gainesville activist and Nixon supporter Chanae Jackson.

But after Democrats failed to win any statewide races Tuesday, the party remains at a crossroads about its future — and the extent to which it will embrace Nixon as its new center.

Nixon was underestimated by her own party and Florida Republicans from the very first day of her Senate campaign.

The back-bench state lawmaker had never run for statewide office and represented the left-most wing of a party that carried little power against Florida's Republican supermajority in the state Legislature.

She was largely overlooked when she announced her Senate run in January, and raised less than $1 million in the six months that followed.

"I'm a community organizer and community organizers don't oftentimes — especially in the state of Florida — actually win elections," she said at the beginning of this year.

Nixon shocked Florida's political establishment when she won her primary in August despite "favoritism," as she described it to the Times/Herald over the summer, for her opponent from the Democratic Party.

She's now maybe the best-known Florida Democrat in the country, with progressive-left campaign priorities like Medicare for All and universal childcare.

Her candidacy marked a sharp departure from recent centrist statewide Democratic candidates intended to appeal to Republicans in a state where Democrats have a massive voter registration disadvantage.

After the turnout successes of her campaign, some of her closest supporters are calling for a reckoning within the party that prioritizes the leadership of progressive Black women like Nixon.

"There's a lot of anti-Blackness in the Democratic Party," Jackson, the Gainesville supporter, said Tuesday. "They can no longer continue to have our labor and then not accept our leadership."

Florida Democratic Party chairwoman Nikki Fried — a moderate Democrat who has clashed with Nixon at various points — said Tuesday that she has no plans to leave her leadership post anytime soon as she, too, looks ahead to the next election.

"Nope, not on the table," she said Tuesday afternoon, when asked about the possibility of new leadership. "My term ends in 2028."

But she and Democrats across the ideological spectrum agree that Nixon's presence on Tuesday's ballot was a rising tide that lifted other Democratic candidates.

"What Angie's been able to do is energize the base, give a compelling argument of why vote Dem this cycle, and we've seen a lot more lower-propensity voters turning out in this midterm," Fried said.

Nixon still had her skeptics in the party, even as it was near universally recognized that she drove more voters to the polls.

"Angie Nixon's campaigns have certainly energized a large segment of Democrats," Miami-Dade Democratic Chairwoman Laura Kelley said last week. "There is a positive, and at the same time there are people who legitimately think she may be too extreme."

Republicans had spent most of the campaign framing Nixon as a "radical" threat to the country because of her recent decision to join the Democratic Socialists of America among other minor parties this summer. But she beat Moody in Miami-Dade, home to scores of voters who fled socialist governments, and did just as well as centrist Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly.

"A lot of Democrats who were panicking about Angie Nixon on the ballot on primary night are instead gonna be thanking their lucky stars that she ended up being the candidate," Democratic pollster Fernand Amandi said ahead of the election.

While Nixon lost Tuesday, she came within three points of Moody — after getting little investment from national Democratic funding groups, compared to the tens of millions poured into winning Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.

Some supporters point to the fact that she was in striking distance at all as evidence that real investment from the party, and belief a candidate like Nixon could have won, could have made a difference.

"Her loss is 100% on the national and state parties. If she'd had even a modicum of support, she could have won," former Miami-Dade County Democratic Party Chairman Robert Dempster said Tuesday night.

Nixon herself agreed to reporters Tuesday night that more investment might have made a difference in her race, but she focused her sights ahead: "At the end of the day, it's OK."

Since Moody is fulfilling Secretary of State Marco Rubio's term, she needs to run for reelection for a full term in 2028. For Nixon, the campaign's already begun.

"I'm looking forward to registering voters these next two years," she said. What she hopes people take away from Tuesday as 2028 looms is that, "Florida is not a lost cause, and I think we proved that tonight."

images.caption: Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon lost a close race for U.S. Senate against GOP incumbent Ashley Moody.

articles.title: Catholic preschools’ lawyer sees a Supreme Court win
articles.summary: Watch The Gavel Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 3 p.m. EST as we talk with Nick Sansone, an attorney at Public Citizen leading the legal challenge to President Trump’s arch. Tune in! Nick Reaves thinks he just got his first win arguing before the Supreme Court. “I feel confident!” Reaves told The Gavel moments after…
articles.body:
Watch The Gavel Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 3 p.m. EST as we talk with Nick Sansone , an attorney at Public Citizen leading the legal challenge to President Trump’s arch. Tune in!

Nick Reaves thinks he just got his first win arguing before the Supreme Court.

“I feel confident!” Reaves told The Gavel moments after he stepped out of the courtroom for one of the biggest cases of the term.

The first-time Supreme Court oral advocate and his team at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty represent Catholic parishes and parents in their fight for an exemption from a Colorado mandate that preschools must accept kids of same-sex couples if they want to receive public funds.

They argue the mandate violates the First Amendment.

“The headline from the other side is all about exclusion, but at the end of the day, that’s really not what’s actually happening on the ground,” Reaves said. “On the ground, this is about ensuring Catholic families can be equal participants in this program.”

Long before he stepped up to the lectern on Tuesday morning, many court watchers expected Reaves would walk away with a win at the Supreme Court. Still, as he appeared to garner sympathy with the court’s conservatives during the two-hour session, the contrasting pushback from the liberal justices was stark.

“Your rule is, like, not allowing our society to have all people live together,” said Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson .

Justice Elena Kagan looked up to the ceiling at one point, gesturing with her hands as she warned the legal rule the parishes and the Trump administration have requested would “put ourselves in the middle of” hot-button religious disputes that “could go on forever.” Justice Sonia Sotomayor flatly told Reaves he was asking for “a right to reject children.”

“If it’s a sincere religious exercise to exclude Blacks, this principle would permit the exclusion of those Black children?” she pressed.

The hypotheticals came as no surprise. The Catholic preschools have long pointed to how the court has long held racial classifications to exacting scrutiny. They say they’re asking for nothing new, and the warnings from the other side won’t actually become problems.

“The sky hasn’t fallen,” Reaves told us.

He noted critics voiced similar concerns when Becket convinced the Supreme Court to rule that cities can’t refuse to contract with a Catholic foster care group because it wouldn’t certify same-sex couples, a case named Fulton v. City of Philadelphia .

“I think it’s actually telling that you have a lot of the same amicus coming in this case saying the sky is going to fall,” Reaves said. “They said that seven years ago in Fulton, and the sky didn’t fall.”

In that case, three conservative justices — Clarence Thomas , Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch — were ready to go further than the majority and overrule a key 1990 precedent that has led courts to uphold laws that burden religious rights, if they are neutral and generally applicable.

So, the trio was expected to be friendly voices for Reaves’ argument. They were indeed.

Gorsuch, for instance, said he struggled to see the concerns voiced by the liberal justices that a win for the Catholic parishes would be the “end of the world.”

“That seems to me to be problematic to suggest, ‘oh, my goodness, it would be a sea change to do what we do in almost every case,” Gorsuch said.

Still, Reaves needs a majority of at least five.

If the liberal justices all vote against him, he can only afford to lose one vote from the other conservatives: Chief Justice John Roberts , Justice Brett Kavanaugh and Justice Amy Coney Barrett .

Kavanaugh told Colorado it could be a “win-win” if they back off their mandate. Barrett questioned whether same-sex couples had actually been turned away from a preschool. The most difficult questioning among that trio arguably came from Roberts, who began by wondering if there was a “significant difference” from the precedents Reaves relies on. Reaves didn’t seem too worried, particularly after the chief warned Colorado’s lawyer they seemed “quite anxious” to bury another past Supreme Court decision.

“I think he’s a good questioner. He asks both sides the hardest question,” Reaves told us.

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams. Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

Judge probing DOJ conduct in golf course case: A federal judge is opening an investigation into whether the Trump administration may have lied to her in the ongoing litigation over Trump’s plan to overhaul the golf courses at East Potomac Park. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes says she’ll conduct it herself or appoint a special master.

Case against ex-FBI officials dismissed: U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui has dismissed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about the bureau’s investigations into Hunter Biden’s laptop, finding no probable cause to support charges in what he cast as a political prosecution.

New Comey charges in limbo: U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden is weighing former FBI Director James Comey’s request to have a third criminal case against him thrown out . Comey has not been indicted by a grand jury on the new charges, which allege that he disclosed sensitive national defense information to the media a decade ago.

Defamation suit against Wall Street Journal tossed, again: U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles of Miami has permanently dismissed Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal for publishing a story about an alleged letter the president sent Jeffrey Epstein for his 50 th birthday. It’s the second time a judge found Trump failed to prove the newspaper acted with “actual malice.”

SCOTUS sets January arguments : The Supreme Court has revealed which cases it will hear when the new year begins in January. A civil contempt fight between Apple and a major video game developer, a trademark strength dispute involving PepsiCo, the constitutionality of six-person juries and more are on the calendar.

Another Dan Sullivan: The Supreme Court admitted “Daniel J. Sullivan” to the bar on Election Day. No, not that one. And no, not that one either. Yes, it was yet a third Dan Sullivan. It gave both Justice Brett Kavanaugh and Justice Elena Kagan a laugh.

No show: A panel of judges waited 30 minutes for Ada Brown, a federal judge in the Northern District of Texas who was suspended for not agreeing to her colleagues’ demands to undergo mental fitness testing, to show up for a hearing last Friday focused on allegations that she made racist remarks from the bench and abandoned her post. She never did. Read the transcript .

Polls are closed. Election litigation not so much.

So far, the Trump administration has faced a string of losses.

The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Justice Department’s (DOJ) emergency request to set aside 20,000 mail ballots it says were sent to likely noncitizens in California.

A lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses was also thrown out . And a federal judge in D.C. ruled that the government’s attempts to “impose new procedures for counting ballots, through threats of criminal prosecution of state election officials” are unconstitutional.

Ahead of the election, the Trump administration shifted its strategy.

“We are deploying election monitors in California and across the country to observe compliance with federal law, charging election fraudsters daily, and will pursue other legal avenues to ensure that only eligible American citizens vote,” a DOJ spokesperson told The Gavel on Tuesday morning.

The Justice Department later confirmed it had sent about 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states for the first time to watch the polls. Despite fears, their presence seemingly caused little disruption, with watchdogs noting only isolated incidents of “concerning behavior” in a few states that were quickly resolved.

The Trump administration’s demands have largely focused on claims of noncitizen voting.

It sent letters, including to California and Washington, that requested states’ check their voter rolls for potential ineligible voters, sequester ballots suspected to be cast by noncitizens and not count them until citizenship status can be verified.

States refused and courts agreed. So, the ballots are being counted.

What followed on Tuesday was a massive blue wave that saw Democrats flip control of both the House and Senate in a stunning rebuke of President Trump.

More litigation could arise, as states now prepare to certify their elections in the weeks ahead.

“We’ve seen even before election day, this administration making wild, false claims to try to sow doubt in the election results before anyone had even cast a ballot, and we expect that the administration and many of their allies will continue to do so in the coming days,” Andrew Walchuk, the senior policy director and counsel for voting and fair representation at Common Cause said on Tuesday night. “We are prepared to respond.”

But the shift in power in Congress will make it more difficult for Republicans to challenge the results, and late Tuesday night, Trump told the New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept them.

It had been a mixed bag for the administration so far in the courts.

The 9 th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a lower court ruling that barred the Justice Department from threatening election officials with criminal prosecution if its ballot demands aren’t met. The court agreed 6-5 to reinstate a divided panel’s ruling that described the DOJ’s investigative steps as “core Executive functions.”

And remember, that’s the same court where a divided three-judge panel had sided against the administration in the ballot segregation phase.

Chief Judge Mary Marguia , an Obama appointee, wrote in a dissenting opinion on the election workers case that those two rulings “cannot be reconciled” because the executive branch has “no right” to dictate state election procedures.

The Trump administration’s demand is based on lists comparing voter rolls with federal immigration records. It claims that tens of thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in California alone, but opponents have questioned the veracity of that list, and lower court judges have found it isn’t credible or reliable.

An outside analysis conducted by the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights — which is actively suing the administration — found that more than 40 percent of the names flagged as noncitizens on DOJ’s list were not registered. The department pushed for criminal contempt sanctions, accusing the group of “political grandstanding” in a way that has nothing to do with its legal standing.

Chief Judge James Boasberg , an Obama appointee who sits on the federal bench in D.C., on Tuesday rejected the DOJ’s arguments that the immigration group violated his order.

Facing setbacks, federal prosecutors have instead turned their focus to pursuing individual criminal charges.

On Monday alone, the Justice Department announced charges against 63 individuals for illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration and related crimes. That brought its nine-week total to at least 195 noncitizens charged across 25 states, officials said, and the numbers have kept climbing in the days since.

“If you vote illegally in this country, and you are NOT eligible to vote, @DHSgov will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote Tuesday morning on the social platform X.

Petitions for the Supreme Court to take up cases we are keeping a close eye on this week…

Kidnapping with a car: Congress has limited police power. It has made kidnapping a federal offense by invoking its authority to regulate interstate commerce. So, the statute requires proof the defendant used a “means, facility, or instrumentality” of interstate commerce to qualify. After Alabama charged Derick Brown with murdering a 3-year-old girl, federal prosecutors brought a kidnapping charge against him. They say it qualifies because he was driving a car. Brown wants the Supreme Court to rule that it isn’t automatically a federal offense when an automobile was involved that isn’t proven to have crossed state lines. The case is Brown v. United States .

Alabama redistricting: The fate of Alabama’s congressional map for future election cycles is in the Supreme Court’s hands. In 2023, the justices struck down a design with only one majority-Black district. Republicans redesigned it, but their new version still doesn’t outright create a second district. They say that’s allowed, particularly after the Supreme Court narrowed the Voting Rights Act earlier this year. The court allowed Republicans to use their design for the midterms, but the ruling is technically temporary. Now, Alabama wants the court to effectively make it permanent by summarily reversing a lower ruling that remains on the books. The cases are Allen v. Caster , Allen v. Milligan and Allen v. Singleton.

The justices are also still sitting on several petitions we highlighted in previous editions:

The First Amendment challenge to California’s implicit bias requirement for medical education courses

Baseball legend Roberto Clemente’s sons’ fight against Puerto Rico officials

A case at the intersection of bankruptcy and arbitration law

Qualified immunity battles stemming from a Michigan police shooting and a Minnesota George Floyd protest

A thorny battle over a Louisiana city’s liability

A civil rights lawsuit against the Massachusetts Institute of Technology alleging antisemitism.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Guerrero v. Johnson , a case concerning when prisoners can file a second attempt to secure release via what is known as a habeas petition.

Daniel Alejandro Moreno-Gama , accused of throwing a Molotov cocktail at OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ‘s home in San Francisco in April, will appear in court for a preliminary hearing.

A status conference will be held in federal court in D.C. for Brian Cole Jr ., the man accused of planting pipe bombs outside the Democratic and Republican National Committee party headquarters on the eve of Jan. 6, 2021.

A federal judge in Rhode Island will hold a remote hearing to consider granting partial summary judgment in a case brought by Democratic state attorneys general challenging the attachment of immigration enforcement conditions on federal victim assistance grants.

A New York appeals court will hear oral arguments in Trump’s latest bid to overturn his conviction on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records for concealing payments to adult film actress Stormy Daniels.

A motion hearing will be held in Davidson County, Tenn., for a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the state’s lethal injection protocol that was brought over a year before the botched execution of death row inmate Christa Pike.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor will participate in a discussion on civics education with the CEO of iCivics, Louise Dubé , at an annual symposium hosted by the George Washington Presidential Library in Mount Vernon, Va.

The Supreme Court will release an orders list.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Neilsen v. Watanabe , a case deciding whether a federal prisoner can sue prison officials for monetary damages under the Bivens precedent for denying him adequate medical care, and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. , which focuses on how just compensation is calculated when a private company conducts eminent domain under the Natural Gas Act.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC , a case to determine whether the Labor Department can use in-house tribunals to fine employers who violate certain visa rules.

The 9 th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will hear oral arguments in the Justice Department’s appeal of a lower court order that blocked a ban on transgender troops in the military.

articles.title: Let us build: Permitting reform can’t wait
articles.summary: It’s time to stop gambling with the futures of hardworking LIUNA members and get this bill passed.
articles.body:
The Laborers’ International Union of North America , known by the acronym LIUNA, represents more than 540,000 skilled workers who are proud to build the United States and Canada. They build our highways, bridges and schools. They power the country with wind, solar, nuclear, hydropower and pipelines.

Put simply: LIUNA builds North America. We take pride in delivering projects safely, on time and on budget. But too often, that work gets politicized, delayed or cancelled.

For decades, outdated permitting laws have been used as weapons to block critical projects. The SunZia wind and transmission project waited 17 years for the green light. The Atlantic Coast Pipeline sat stalled for six years before it was cancelled in 2020 . They’re two of many.

Approvals can take years, then vanish with the stroke of a pen. Projects that are permitted, financed and ready to break ground sit in court longer than it would take our members to build them.

To some, that’s a number on a spreadsheet. To LIUNA members, it’s another day without a paycheck, health coverage or pension credit. Construction workers are paid by the hour, and so are their benefits. They build careers by completing one project and moving on to another. When projects stop, families pay the price.

Our members can’t afford this instability. That’s why LIUNA supports Sen. Martin Heinrich’s (D-N.M.) Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act .

It sets clear deadlines for court challenges. It narrows and adds transparency to environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act . And it gives our members the certainty they’ve needed for years. It also protects good union jobs, prevailing wages, apprenticeships and the safeguards that protect workers and communities, all while lowering energy costs for every American.

For more than a decade, LIUNA has testified, filed comments and backed permitting bills, only to watch them die in the final hours of a congressional session. This time, we have a real shot. It’s time to stop gambling with the futures of hardworking LIUNA members and get this bill passed.

Brent Booker is the general president of the Laborers’ International Union of North America.

articles.title: Democrat Nathan Johnson flips Texas attorney general’s office
articles.summary: Texans elected a Democrat to serve as the state’s top lawyer for the first time in decades on Tuesday, flipping an attorney general’s office that had become a reliable conservative stronghold under outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Nathan Johnson, a state senator from Dallas, is poised to become Texas’s first Democratic attorney general in…
articles.body:
Texans elected a Democrat to serve as the state’s top lawyer for the first time in decades on Tuesday, flipping an attorney general’s office that had become a reliable conservative stronghold under outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Nathan Johnson, a state senator from Dallas, is poised to become Texas’s first Democratic attorney general in 32 years after defeating Mayes Middleton.

Johnson earned 53.4 percent of the vote to Middleton’s 46.6 percent, with nearly all of the ballots counted as of Wednesday morning, according to Decision Desk HQ .

“This is a tremendous honor, and a tremendous responsibility,” Johnson wrote on the social platform X . “Texans voted for an attorney general who will represent them and the interest of our state, and who will above all uphold the rule of law. That’s what I intend to do.”

Johnson portrayed himself as the antithesis of Paxton, campaigning on a “back to basics” approach that would restore the office’s focus on public safety, consumer protection and investigating corruption. He also pledged to be a legal stopgap against what he described as “the MAGA machine’s assault” on individual rights and overreach from the Trump administration.

It’s a dramatic shift for the largest state attorney general’s office in the South, which aggressively pursued legal action against the Obama and Biden administrations. A Texas Tribune analysis found Paxton and his predecessor sued the Obama administration nearly 50 times over the former president’s two terms, and the office’s own records indicate more than 100 lawsuits filed during Biden’s term.

Middleton, meanwhile, had tied himself closely to President Trump, promising to continue advancing an “America First” legal strategy that focused on border security, defending abortion restrictions and rooting out fraud, waste and abuse in the government, among other conservative issues.

Johnson’s victory was part of a larger blue wave that swept Texas in the midterms, with Democrat Gina Hinojosa taking the governor’s mansion and Democrat James Talarico flipping a Senate seat for the first time in more than 30 years.

articles.title: Trump: Iran war partially to blame for GOP midterm losses
articles.summary: President Trump partially blamed the ongoing war with Iran for the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses in the midterms — but said he would have done it again. Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Middle East conflict, now in its eighth month, “was a piece of it” in an election night interview. Gas and…
articles.body:
President Trump partially blamed the ongoing war with Iran for the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses in the midterms — but said he would have done it again.

Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Middle East conflict, now in its eighth month, “was a piece of it” in an election night interview .

Gas and diesel prices have skyrocketed in the U.S. and globally since the war started in late February, increasing voter frustrations after the president campaigned on ending foreign wars in 2024. Trump told the Journal that he thought high fuel costs were the biggest factor behind his party’s losses Tuesday.

Republicans suffered a historically large defeat in Tuesday’s midterms, losing at least seven Senate seats, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected. Two races, Mississippi and Alaska, remain uncalled as of Wednesday morning.

The GOP also lost 30 seats in the House, with more than 20 races left to be projected, according to DDHQ.

Some of the Republican candidates who faltered were ones handpicked or endorsed by Trump himself. These candidates include Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who lost to Democrat James Talarico by 12 points, and South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham (R), who lost in an upset to Democrat Annie Andrews by 4 points.

The president backed Paxton in his primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and supported Graham in a special primary after urging South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) to tap her to fill the seat left open by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R).

He told the Journal that he could “only do so much” to help Republican candidates, admitting some had “flaws.”

“I tried to help them,” Trump said of Graham and Paxton. “Darline worked very hard, they worked hard. But they both didn’t make it.”

At the start of next year, the administration will be met with a more hostile Congress than what he has faced during the first two years of his term.

Trump told the Journal that he was willing to work with Democrats — similar to his sentiment after the 2018 midterms — but pointed out he retains the ability to veto any bills passed through Congress in the final two years of his presidency.

“I think we’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll get along very well with them,” he said. “If we don’t, we’ll be very tough on them, they’ll be very tough on us.”

The president also told the Journal and The New York Times that he would accept the results of the election, after warning of widespread fraud and cheating by his opponents in years past.

articles.title: Iran’s Khamenei warns Trump loss at polls won’t end US hostility
articles.summary: Iranian supreme leader says US policy won’t change amid Tehran ‘Fight Against Global Arrogance’ day rallies
articles.body:
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has said that anyone expecting a shift in the United States’ policy towards his country is “seriously mistaken”, hours after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump.

“Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Khamenei said in a written statement published on his website.

Iran’s head of state, who has not appeared publicly since his father and predecessor Ali Khamenei was assassinated in a US-Israeli attack on his office in February, said Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz had shattered the “myth of America’s invincibility” and warned that any renewed US attack would draw a far wider response .

Khamenei’s statement came on the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, which Iran marks each year as the “National Day of the Fight Against Global Arrogance”.

“In the event of repeated transgression, it will take on much wider dimensions,” he said, warning that any renewed US attacks on Iran could lead to a wider conflict.

Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran that began in February likely impacted his Republican Party’s poor performance in the elections, but argued that voters were reacting to higher petrol prices rather than the military campaign itself.

“I don’t think it’s the war,” he told Fox News on Tuesday. “I think it’s the gasoline prices.”

“People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequences of paying more for gasoline.”

Trump also left open the possibility of a major new attack on Iran, telling the Fox & Friends programme on Tuesday that some people were pushing for what he described as a “heavy hit”.

“A lot of people would like to do the heavy hit. A lot of people wouldn’t,” he said.

Khamenei’s comments came as another top Iranian official struck a more conciliatory tone on Wednesday following the results of the US vote, which saw Democrats score a historic victory by taking control of both chambers of Congress.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” said Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator with Washington and his country’s parliament speaker.

“If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added on X.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser and assistant to the supreme leader, said Trump had been “slapped in the face by his own people”.

“The true winner in this arena was Iran, which transferred the cost of the war into the United States,” he wrote on X.

But Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, warned that the Democrats’ victory could actually increase the risk of Trump escalating in the short term.

”He has shown a pattern in which, in face of humiliation and defeat, he becomes more reckless,” he said, adding that Trump could respond to the election by ramping up attacks against Iran out of “pure revenge”.

Parsi warned that the period between now and January, before Democrats take control of Congress, could be particularly volatile, as that’s when Democrats could try to use their new majority to restrict funding for the war.

“The combination of him running out of time and him becoming more reckless as a result of a defeat creates a very dangerous period for the next two months,” he said.

The US has warned it could carry out a short but intensive military campaign against Iran after the midterms.

Hamidreza Moghadamfar, an adviser to the commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Iran would hit targets beyond US bases if Gulf states allowed Washington to launch attacks from their territory. Speaking at a rally in Bandar Abbas, he named the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain and said Iran would respond with a “new doctrine and new technology”.

Trump said the US was prepared to act, but suggested another attack might not be necessary as hopes for a negotiated solution linger.

“I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it,” he said in an interview with the Financial Times.
