articles.title: When the disaster is no longer temporary, relief shouldn’t be either
articles.summary: Congress should establish a formal process for when an emergency becomes a protracted national crisis.
articles.body:
On Aug. 20, the United States deported more than 160 people to Haiti on the first removal flight since the government ended temporary protected status, or TPS, for approximately 350,000 Haitians. That plane, which included some former TPS holders, landed in Cap-Haïtien rather than the capital Port-au-Prince, because continuing insecurity has made the airport too dangerous for U.S. commercial flights.

TPS allows eligible foreign nationals already in the U.S. to remain and work legally when conditions in their home country prevent safe return. Haiti’s 2010 earthquake, which killed more than 220,000 people and displaced 1.5 million , seemed to fit the model.

For 15 years, successive administrations renewed or redesignated Haiti for temporary protection. But this June, after a lengthy legal battle culminating in a Supreme Court decision, Haitians lost their protection.

Advocates and critics of TPS point to the same 15-year duration as evidence for their positions. Both sides overlook a more fundamental question: What should we do when the disaster becomes chronic?

My parents immigrated from Haiti to the United States in the 1980s. Their story is not a TPS story, but it taught me that migration often begins long before disaster strikes. My work has reinforced that lesson.

I lead the development of networks — subsea and terrestrial — that connect people and economies. I think a lot about resilience, redundancy and a system’s capacity to absorb failure. A well-designed network should be able to lose a link and reroute. But when recovery is incomplete, the system becomes more vulnerable and, without sufficient investment, may never return to full capacity.

According to the Internal Displacement Monitoring Center, between 2008 and 2023, 44 natural disasters triggered approximately 2.9 million internal displacements in Haiti, against a population of roughly 10 million. The country has rarely had time to recover before the next shock.

Meanwhile, successive Haitian governments have contended with political instability, state capture by elites and chronic underinvestment, particularly in rural infrastructure, where barely 1 in 10 people have electricity. By the mid-2010s, roughly 80 percent of urban households relied primarily on charcoal, increasing the demand for wood across an already stressed landscape and accelerating migration toward cities that lacked the jobs, housing and public institutions to absorb it.

This trajectory has become familiar worldwide as climate and natural disasters collide with already stressed systems. Instead of its current approach of temporary renewals or terminations based on the latest country assessment, Congress should establish a formal process for when an emergency becomes a protracted national crisis.

I propose a two-step national stability review, conducted jointly by the Departments of Homeland Security and State, that would be triggered whenever a country has been designated for TPS for 10 consecutive years. The country-level review, with its findings published, would answer fundamentally different questions than Homeland Security seeks to answer today. Not whether the conditions that triggered the crisis or the current TPS designation persist, but rather whether their persistence means the crisis has become chronic.

A chronic situation could be determined by measuring the severity and durability of the conditions, whether environmental and climate shocks compound them, whether it is feasible to safely return within a designated period and whether institutional capacity can support returnees.

Not every protracted crisis would result in a designation. But if the country review finds the conditions have become chronic, a second-stage individual assessment would follow for people who have held TPS status continuously for 10 years. Only those demonstrating durable economic, community or family ties to the U.S. would become eligible to apply for permanent residence, subject to criminal, security and admissibility screening. Neither assessment on its own would be sufficient.

The review would intentionally limit eligibility to those with a substantial history of temporary protection and deep rootedness in the U.S., thereby matching the relief to the nature of the problem and ensuring selectivity.

Congress has provided permanent relief for specific populations and has considered broader legislation such as the American Dream and Promise Act . However, those have generally been limited to a nationality and a specific amnesty date and promised permanent status. A national stability review would ask whether TPS remains the appropriate legal instrument given the nature and persistence of the crisis.

The United States cannot offer a right to permanent residency to the billions of people who experience environmental vulnerability, weak infrastructure or poor governance. A national stability review would neither admit new migrants nor automatically convert anyone’s status, but it would end the practice of renewing protection for a decade or more and then suddenly declaring the country healed or, worse, signaling that we no longer care whether it is.

Fifteen years of temporary protection isn’t merely evidence of political paralysis; it is evidence that in many cases, it is no longer logical to call a crisis temporary. An earthquake or hurricane ends. But a country where planes cannot safely land in its capital has already made the case that it is experiencing system-level failures.

Congress should recognize the difference between acute emergencies and structural fragility and create a more nuanced humanitarian pathway for when the next disaster becomes a chronic condition.

Alex-Handrah Aimé is vice president of Network Investments at Meta, where she focuses on the subsea and terrestrial infrastructure that connects data centers and provides connectivity to billions of users. She was born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti and is a PD Soros Fellow and a 2026 Public Voices Fellow with the OpEd Project.

articles.title: Susie Lee wins reelection to Nevada House seat
articles.summary: Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.) is projected to win reelection to a fifth term Tuesday, defeating Republican Marty O’Donnell in the closely watched race, adding to Democrats’ sweeping Election Day victories, according to Decision Desk HQ. The race in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District was called early Wednesday morning, with Lee leading O’Donnell nearly 60 percent to…
articles.body:
Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.) is projected to win reelection to a fifth term Tuesday, defeating Republican Marty O’Donnell in the closely watched race, adding to Democrats’ sweeping Election Day victories , according to Decision Desk HQ .

The race in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District was called early Wednesday morning, with Lee leading O’Donnell nearly 60 percent to 38.6 percent and nearly all ballots counted.

Lee’s victory keeps the district in Democrats hands, two years after she narrowly won reelection despite President Trump winning the district by less than 1 percentage point in 2024.

The region, which encompasses parts of Las Vegas and southern Clark County, had been a perennial Republican target. Lee won her previous race with roughly 51.4 percent of the vote.

The Democrat, who has served in Congress since 2019, made affordability a centerpiece of her campaign, emphasizing the rising costs of housing and healthcare . She also touted her bipartisan work on water conservation and protecting Nevada’s economy.

She also held a significant fundraising advantage heading into Election Day, bringing in $5.6 million to her campaign, including $1.2 million during the third quarter, according to the filings.

Republicans appeared to pull back from the contest in the final stretch. Safety and Affordability PAC, a group backed by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., canceled $1 million in planned television advertising for O’Donnell after initially reserving $3 million, the Nevada Independent reported in October.

The move came as the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race in Democrats’ favor, suggesting the seat had become increasingly difficult for Republicans to flip.

O’Donnell, a former video game composer best known for his work on the “Halo” and “Destiny” franchises, secured the Republican nomination in June with Trump’s endorsement. He campaigned on tightening border security and protecting American jobs amid the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence.

articles.title: Ohio’s Amy Acton stops speech to help person in crowd after historic win
articles.summary: Democratic Governor-elect Amy Acton paused to help someone in the crowd Tuesday night.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton paused to help someone in the crowd Tuesday night after claiming victory in Ohio’s gubernatorial race, a moment captured during her election night celebration and quickly shared on social media. The gesture came as supporters gathered to mark a historic night for the former public health director.

You can hear someone from the crowd yell, “We need a medic, we need a medic.” Acton’s mouth dropped as she looked out at the crowd and said to the audience, “Someone passed out, we’re going to hold for a minute.”

Acton then exited the stage and swiftly moved into the crowd toward the person whom they believed had fainted. No additional information about the individual is available at this time.

Watch Acton’s full acceptance speech below. (The incident happens at about the 8:30 mark.)

It was a big night for Acton as she became Ohio’s first female governor and the state’s first Democratic governor in two decades. Her campaign centered on lowering costs for families, improving education and reducing healthcare expenses.

NewsNation reported that the race drew national attention in its final weeks after a controversial advertisement featuring Acton’s estranged mother sparked bipartisan backlash. The campaign also featured sharp clashes over the state’s pandemic response and Ohio’s political future.

A former state health director, Acton rose to prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic and won the governor’s office in one of the most expensive and hard-fought campaigns in state history.

articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has bucked his party in recent years, said Tuesday’s midterm blowout by Democrats was “about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises.”

“Tonight’s outcome isn’t about placing faith in Democrats or socialist principles; it’s about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises,” Massie said Tuesday night on the social platform X .

“All Republicans had to do was: 1. put Americans First 2. not start another war 3. prosecute sex traffickers,” he added.

A blue wave swept across the U.S. on Tuesday, with the Democrats winning both the House and Senate majorities and securing a chance of restricting President Trump’s power until the end of his second term.

The Democrats’ victories came amid rocky political territory for the GOP, with Republicans weighed down by issues including the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval numbers and concerns about the cost of living.

Democrats are projected to end up with 257 seats in the House and 55 seats in the Senate , according to Decision Desk HQ, marking gains for the party that currently holds 214 seats in the lower chamber and 45 seats in the upper.

In September, Massie, who lost his primary to an opponent supported by Trump, predicted a backlash toward the president and his party in this year’s midterm elections.

“I think his comeuppance will happen on Election Day, and the day after I think there’s going to be a reckoning,” Massie, who has been a vocal critic of Trump and his policies, told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins at the time.

Massie has crossed the aisle to back multiple Iran war powers resolutions and spearheaded a bipartisan effort for the release of files linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

articles.title: Mike Johnson not running to lead House GOP after historic midterm losses
articles.summary: Mike Johnson revealed on an all-staff call he will not lead House Republicans in the next Congress as Jim Jordan mounts a minority leader bid.
articles.body: Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., does not plan to lead House Republicans in the next Congress after his razor-thin majority dissolved under a tidal wave of Democrat victories. Johnson revealed the news on an all-staff call on Wednesday morning, Fox News Digital is told by two sources. The development comes shortly after it became public that House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, will mount a bid to be minority leader next year. It's not immediately clear how far in advance Johnson's call was planned. The speaker's remarkable rise to power began with his ascension from relative obscurity to win the gavel in October 2023, following the ouster of ex-Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif. JIM JORDAN THROWS HAT IN RING FOR HOUSE MINORITY LEADER AS GOP PICKS UP PIECES AFTER BLUE WAVE Johnson, who only came to Congress in 2017, had won the unanimous backing of his colleagues after three weeks of chaos that paralyzed the legislative branch where the House was leaderless. He spent the majority of his time in recent months crisscrossing the country for GOP candidates in a bid to keep his leadership spot. But those efforts apparently were not enough to stave off significant losses across both battleground districts and seats that were considered Republican strongholds. DEM PROBES COULD ‘TORTURE’ YOUNG TRUMP OFFICIALS WITH CRUSHING LEGAL BILLS, SUBPOENAED CONSERVATIVE WARNS Among the most stunning losses projected Tuesday night include Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., and Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind. National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C., is also expected to lose his race despite leading the House GOP campaign arm. Johnson conceded the House was lost at his election night party in his hometown of Shreveport, Louisiana on Tuesday night. "From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson told the audience. "It's only happened twice in 90 years that a sitting president has picked up or held seats for his party in that first two-year cycle, and there's a lot of reasons for it. It's very, very difficult to overcome. And it looks like history will be kept tonight." Johnson's No. 3, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., told colleagues he would be running for the whip job in the minority.
